scabbard, whereon the hilt fitted of ivory
shone forth conspicuous among the wondrous arms.
Beside them was stretched along the ground the mighty spear,
like the high-leaved firs of Pelion,
still breathing of the gore and the blood of Hector.
And then among the Argives Thetis of the dark veil
spoke a wondrous word, grieving for Achilles:
“Now indeed all the prizes of the contest are accomplished,
as many as I, greatly grieving for my dead son, laid down;
but let him come forward who saved the body and is best of the Achaeans,
and now I will grant him to wear the marvellous, immortal arms,
which even the blessed immortals greatly admired.”
So she spoke; and they leapt up, contending in words,
the son of Laertes and the son of godlike Telamon,
Ajax, who greatly surpassed all among the Danaans,
as a bright star in the gleaming heaven,
the evening star, which shines far among all the stars;
like it he stood beside the arms of the son of Peleus;
and he asked Idomeneus to judge, and the son of Neleus,
and wise Agamemnon; for these he hoped
knew truly the deeds of the glorious struggle;
and likewise Odysseus altogether trusted in them;
for they were prudent and blameless among the Danaans.
But Nestor to Idomeneus and to the noble son of Atreus,
both desiring it, spoke a word apart from the rest:
“O friends, truly a great trouble and unbearable on this day
the heedless Heavenly Ones bring upon us,
seeing that great Ajax and shrewd Odysseus
are rushing to a strife unbearable and grievous;
for whichever of the two a god grants to win the glory
will rejoice in his heart, but the other will swell with great grief,
blaming all the Danaans, and beyond all the rest
us; nor will that man stand any more among us as before
in the battle; and great sorrow will come to the Achaeans
if dread wrath seizes either of them, since of all
heroes they excel, the one in war, the other in counsel.
But come, obey me, since I am the elder
by far, not a little, and I have, with my great age,
understanding too, because I have toiled through much good and many sorrows;
for always in counsel a wise old man is better
than a younger, since he knows full many things;
therefore let us leave it to the kindly Trojans to judge this
between godlike Ajax and war-loving Odysseus,
whichever of them the foemen most dread,
and who it was that saved the body of the son of Peleus
from the deadly war; for among us are spear-won
many Trojans under fresh-imposed bondage;
these will give a straight judgement upon them,
showing favour to neither, since they hate all the Achaeans
alike, remembering their own evil ruin.”
When he had so spoken, well-armed Agamemnon answered him:
“O old man, since no other more prudent than you
is among us Danaans, neither young nor old,
you who say that the Argives will be pitilessly angered
at that man, whichever of these two the gods hereafter cast down
from victory; for the best are contending against each other;
and within me my heart in my breast yearns for this,
that we should give the office of judgement to the spear-won captives;
for anyone, though wronged, will devise deadly deeds
against the warlike Trojans, but will not turn his wrath on us.”
So he spoke; and they, having one mind in their breasts,
openly refused the grievous task of judgement;
and when they had thus refused, the glorious sons of the Trojans
sat down in the midst, captives of the spear though they were,
that they might set straight the right and the warlike quarrel.
And Ajax in the midst, greatly enraged, spoke his word:
“O Odysseus, dread in mind, what god has deceived your wits
to think yourself equal to me in tireless might?
Do you say that you held back the terrible throng from Achilles
when he was struck down in the dust, when the Trojans came about him,
at the time when I sent grievous slaughter upon them
while you cowered away? For surely your mother bore you
a wretch and a weakling, feebler than I am
by as much as a cur is feebler than the deep-roaring lion;
for there is no battle-abiding heart in your breast,
but cunning and reckless deeds are all your care.
Or have you forgotten this, that when to the holy city of Ilium
you shrank from coming with the gathered Achaeans,
and you cowering, unwilling to follow,
the sons of Atreus brought you? Would you had never come!
For by your devisings the famous son of Poeas
we left in holy Lemnos, groaning greatly;
and not on him alone did you plot baneful outrage,
but on godlike Palamedes too you brought destruction,
who was better than you in strength and in wise counsel.
And now you have dared even to come against me,
neither remembering my kindness, nor at all in your heart
holding in awe one far better than yourself, who in the fray
saved you before, when you trembled at the tumult
of the enemy, when the others, leaving you alone in the battle,
abandoned you in the throng of foes, fleeing, you yourself too;
would that in that fight my bold strength
Zeus himself had scared from heaven, that the Trojans
with their two-edged swords might have cut you limb from limb
for a feast to their dogs, and you would not, against my will,
have dared to come and face me, trusting in your guile.
Wretch, why, boasting to be far the mightiest of others
in strength, do you keep your ships in the midst, while in your heart
you dared not, as I did, to drag the swift ships
outside? For fear came upon you. Nor did you ward off
the terrible fire from the ships; but I with fearless heart
stood both against the fire and against Hector, who yielded to me
everywhere in the battle; but you ever feared him exceedingly.
Would that some one had set this contest between us in war,
when the strife arose over fallen Achilles,
that you might have seen me, out of the foe and the grievous tumult,
bearing the fair arms to the huts
together with warlike Achilles himself; but now, trusting
in the cunning of words, you reach for great deeds;
for there is no strength in you to put on the tireless arms
of warlike Aeacides, nor to wield the great spear
in your hands; but for me all things are fashioned
fitting, and it becomes me to bear the splendid arms,
in no way bringing shame on the god's beautiful gifts.
But why do we stand here wrangling with evil words
over the splendid arms of blameless Achilles?
But come, let us make trial with bronze spears
which is the better in man-destroying battle;
for this is a prize of valour in war, not of grievous
words, that silver-footed Thetis set in the midst;
but the need of words belongs to men in the assembly;
for I know that I am far nobler and braver
than you; and my lineage is that whence great Achilles sprang.”
So he spoke; and grievously, with words flung crosswise, answered him
the son of Laertes, wielding his cunning wiles:
“Ajax of measureless speech, why do you say so much to me in vain?
You called me good for nothing and grievous and a weakling
to be, who boast to be far higher than you
in counsels and in words, which increase men's strength;
for even the sheer rock, unbreakable though it is,
stonecutters undercut in the mountains by their craft
with ease, and by craft the great loud-roaring sea
the sailors cross over, when it surges immensely;
and by their skills huntsmen master strong lions
and leopards and boars and the tribes of other beasts;
and bulls of mighty spirit are tamed beneath the yokes
by the will of men; and all things are accomplished by mind.
Always, in every labour and in counsel, a man of much knowledge
is better than a senseless man;
therefore the bold son of Oeneus, knowing me to be wise,
chose me out of all as his helper, that I might come
to the watchmen; and a great deed we both accomplished together;
and it was I who brought the famous son of mighty Peleus
to the sons of Atreus, a helper; and if there be need
of another hero among the Argives,
he will not come by your hands, nor by the counsels
of the other Argives, but I alone of the Achaeans
will bring him, persuading him with gentle words
to the strife of warriors; for great is the power of speech to men
when it is cared for with good sense; but manhood
is fruitless, and a man's great size grows to nothing,
if prudent wisdom does not attend it.
But to me the immortals gave both strength alike and wisdom,
and made me a great help to the Argives.
Nor, as you said, did you save me fleeing before
from the foeman's battle-cry; for I did not flee, but stood my ground firm
against all the rushing Trojans together; and they poured upon me
raging in their might; but I, by the strength of my hands,
loosed the spirit of many; and you speak no true word;
for it was not me you helped in the fray, but for your own self
you stood, showing favour to yourself, lest someone overcome you with the spear
as you fled from the war. And the ships I dragged into the midst,
not trembling at the fury of the foe, but that I might ever
find some device with the sons of Atreus for the war;
and you set the ships outside; but I myself,
having disfigured my own body with grievous blows,
went into the city of the Trojans, that I might learn
what they were devising over the grievous war.
Nor did I fear the spear of Hector, but I myself too
among the foremost leapt up, eager to do battle
with him, when, trusting in his manhood, he challenged all.
And now over Achilles I have slain far more men
of the enemy than you, and I saved him dead together with his arms.
Nor do I fear your spear, but a grievous
wound still moves about me with its pains, for the sake of these arms,
since I was wounded above the slain Achilles;
and in me too, as in Achilles, is the surpassing blood of Zeus.”
So he spoke; and to him again answered strong Ajax:
“O Odysseus of cunning mind and most grievous of all,
I did not see you toiling there, nor did any other
of the Argives, when the Trojans were eager
to drag off slain Achilles; but I, with spear and might,
loosed the knees of some in the fray, and others I scared
ever rushing upon them; and they fled grievously,
like geese or cranes, on which there rushes
an eagle as they feed on the misty plain;
so the Trojans, cowering before my spear and swift sword,
plunged into Ilium, escaping the great calamity.
But for you, even if strength came upon you then, in no way near me
did you fight against the foe, but somewhere far off you yourself
were toiling among other ranks, not about the body
of godlike Achilles, where the great struggle raged.”
So he spoke; and the cunning heart of Odysseus answered him:
“Ajax, I do not deem myself worse than you,
neither in mind nor in might, even if you are most glorious;
but in mind I am far the superior
to you among the Argives, while in might I am your match,
or even nobler; and this the Trojans too know,
who greatly dread me even when they see me afar.
And you yourself know well my strength, and others too,
from the toilsome wrestling in which I greatly laboured,
when about the tomb of slain Patroclus
the high-souled son of Peleus set the glorious prizes.”
So spoke the famous son of godlike Laertes.
And then the sons of the Trojans judged the grievous strife
of the warriors; and the victory and the immortal arms they gave,
all of one mind, to war-loving Odysseus;
and his heart rejoiced beyond measure; but the people groaned.
And the goodly strength of Ajax was frozen; at once upon him
grievous ruin fell about; and within him all
his blood boiled red, and his bitter gall overflowed,
and his bowels were confounded about his liver; and a grievous
pain came about his heart, and a sharp anguish, rushing
through the foundations of his brain, filled all about
his membranes, and confounded the man's mind;
and fixing his eyes upon the ground he stood
like one unmoving; and about him his comrades
in grief led him to the high-prowed ships,
much entreating him; but he went the last road on foot
unwilling; and close beside him followed his Doom.
But when they had come to the ships and the boundless sea,
and the Argives longed for their supper and for sleep,
then Thetis plunged down into the great sea;
and with her went the other Nereids; and about them
swam many sea-beasts, such as the briny swell breeds.
And they were greatly wroth with cunning Prometheus,
remembering how by his prophecies the son of Cronos
gave Thetis to Peleus, though she wished not to be wedded.
And Cymothoe among them, greatly grieving, spoke aloud:
“Ah me, how that wretch endured worthy sufferings
in the unbreakable bond, when the great eagle
tore at his liver as it grew again, sinking deep into his belly.”
So spoke Cymothoe to the dark-tressed daughters of the sea.
And the sun went down, and the threshing-floors were shadowed
as night rushed on, and the stars were spread over heaven.
And the Argives slept by the long-prowed ships,
overcome by ambrosial sleep and by the sweet
wine which from Crete, from noble Idomeneus,
the sailors had brought over the much-surging sea.
But Ajax, angered at the Argives, neither thought
of sweet supper in his hut, nor did sleep
enfold him, but he plunged raging into his arms;
and he took his sharp sword, and pondered measureless things,
whether he should set fire to the ships and destroy all
the Argives, or alone with the grievous sword
swiftly hew cunning Odysseus limb from limb.
And these things he pondered, and would soon have accomplished them all,
had not the Tritonian cast unbearable madness upon him;
for she cared in her heart for much-enduring Odysseus,
remembering the offerings which he ever steadfastly made her;
therefore she turned the fury of the great son of Telamon
away from the Argives. And he went like a hurricane,
terrible, laden with hateful squalls,
which brings to sailors a portent of chill fear,
when the Pleiad sinks into the streams of tireless Ocean,
cowering before glorious Orion,
stirring up the mist, and the sea rages with the storm;
like it he rushed wherever his limbs bore him.
Everywhere he ran about like a shameless beast,
which darts through the glens of a deep-cragged ravine,
foaming at the jaws and pondering many woes
against dogs or huntsmen who have slain its young,
dragging them out of the caves, while it, roaring about its jaws,
looks if anywhere in the thickets it may still see its dear young;
and whoever meets it then, with its frenzied spirit,
for him the grievous day of life is fulfilled;
so he raged pitilessly, and his black heart boiled within him,
as a cauldron unceasing on the hearth of Hephaestus
seethes with a hiss beneath the blazing fire,
when all about its belly much wood is heated,
at the urging of a servant hastening in his heart,
to singe the bristles of a well-fed hog;
so beneath his breast his huge spirit seethed.
He raged like the boundless sea or the tempest
or the swift might of tireless fire, when ceaselessly
the force of a great wind rages among the mountains,
and all about the boundless forest falls blazing with fire;
so Ajax, pierced in his mighty heart with anguish,
raged grievously; and a measureless foam ran down
from his mouth, and a roaring rose from his jaws;
and the arms clashed about his shoulders, and they who looked on,
all alike, trembled at the war-cry of a single man.
And then from Ocean came golden-reined Dawn;
and Sleep went up to the wide heaven like a breeze,
and met Hera as she was newly going toward Olympus
from holy Tethys, where she had gone the morning before;
and she took and kissed him, because he was her noble son-in-law,
since he had lulled the son of Cronos to rest in his bed
about the peaks of Ida, when he was wroth with the Argives;
and straightway she went to the house of Zeus, while he sped
to the bed of Pasithea; and the tribes of men awoke.
But Ajax, like tireless Orion,
ranged with deadly madness in his breast;
and he leapt among the flocks, like a mighty-spirited lion
overcome by grievous hunger in his savage heart;
and them in the dust, one after another, this way and that,
he cast down, as the might of strong Boreas
pours down the leaves, when, summer ending, it turns to winter;
so Ajax in great fury rushed upon the flocks,
thinking to hurl evil dooms upon the Danaans.
And then Menelaus, standing close beside his brother,
apart from the other Danaans, spoke this word to him:
“This day surely will quickly be a day of ruin for all,
with great Ajax raging in his wits,
who will soon burn the ships and slay us too,
all in our huts, angered over the arms.
Would that Thetis had not set this strife about them,
nor that the son of Laertes had dared to contend with a man
far better, opposing him with foolish heart.
But now we have greatly erred, and some evil god has deceived us;
for when warlike Aeacides had fallen, the bulwark of the war
that alone was left was the goodly strength of Ajax; but now him too
the gods will destroy for us, bringing evil upon us both,
that we may all fill up our cup of unseen destruction.”
When he had so spoken, well-armed Agamemnon answered him:
“Do not now, Menelaus, greatly grieving in your heart,
be wroth with the wise king of the Cephallenians;
for he is not the cause, since very often to us
he proves a good help, and a grief to the foe.”
So the Danaans, in their grief, spoke among themselves.
But far off the shepherds, by the streams of Xanthus,
cowered beneath the tamarisks, escaping the heavy calamity;
as when before a swift eagle hares cower
in the thick bushes, and it near at hand, screaming sharply,
flies hither and thither with outspread wings;
so they, one here, one there, trembled before the mighty man.
At last he stood beside a slaughtered ram,
and laughing a deadly laugh he spoke this word:
“Lie now in the dust, food for dogs and birds;
for not even the glorious arms of Achilles saved you,
for whose sake you, a fool, contended with a far better man;
lie there, dog; for no wedded wife shall ever bewail you,
falling upon you in unbearable grief over a child,
nor your parents; and you shall not be among them as they long for
the goodly blessing of your old age, since far from your homeland
birds and dogs shall tear you, fallen.”
So he spoke, thinking that cunning Odysseus
lay there among the slain, defiled with much blood;
and then the Tritonian scattered from his mind and his eyes
the grim Madness that breathed destruction;
and swiftly she came to the steep streams of Styx,
where the swift Furies dwell, who upon mortals
ever overweening send evil torments.
But Ajax, when he saw the flocks gasping upon the ground,
marvelled utterly in his heart; for he deemed it was a snare
from the blessed ones; and he sank down in all his limbs,
stricken in spirit with anguish; nor could he
for grief step forward or back,
but he stood like a peak that among the mountains
is rooted highest far above all the rest.
But when his spirit gathered again within his breast,
he groaned a grievous groan, and lamented thus:
“Ah me, why am I so hated by the immortals?
They have harmed my wits and laid evil madness upon me,
to slay the flocks, which were no cause of my anger.
Would that I had taken vengeance on the grievous heart of Odysseus
with my own hands, since indeed he cast me into evil ruin,
baleful as he is utterly; but may he suffer sorrows in his heart,
all that the Furies devise for grievous men;
and may they grant to the other Argives too
deadly battles and tearful griefs,
and to Atreus' son Agamemnon himself; nor may he unharmed
come to his own home, much as he longs to arrive.
But why should I, being good, remain among the hateful?
Let the deadly host of the Argives perish; let the unbearable
life perish; for no longer does the good man hold the prize, but the worse
is honoured and more loved; for indeed Odysseus
is honoured among the Argives, while of me they have utterly forgotten,
and of my deeds, all that I did and endured for the host.”
So speaking, the goodly son of mighty Telamon
drove Hector's sword through his neck; and from him the blood
gushed gurgling forth. And he was stretched in the dust
like Typhon, whom the thunderbolts of Zeus consumed;
and all about the black earth groaned greatly as he fell.
And then the Danaans came in a throng, when they saw him
lying in the dust; but before none of them came
near, since fear held all who looked upon him.
But quickly they fell about the slain; and over his head,
fallen prostrate, they poured boundless dust;
and the wailing of their lament reached the divine air;
as when from wool-fleeced ewes men drive off
the little young, that they may make a feast for themselves,
and the mothers leap greatly, bleating without ceasing
for their young about the bereaved folds;
so they about Ajax greatly mourned on that day
all together; and round them shadowy Ida echoed
and the plain and the ships and the boundless sea.
And Teucer about him greatly purposed to draw on his own doom,
grievous; but the others kept him from the great sword.
And he in grief fell upon the dead man,
shedding many tears, more thickly than a little child
who beside the hearth, with ashes flung about his shoulders
and all over his head, laments the orphaned day
of his mother's death, who reared him knowing not his father;
so he wailed for his fallen brother,
creeping about the corpse, and lamented thus:
“Ajax, strong of heart, why was your mind so harmed
that against your own self you cast grievous slaughter and woe?
Was it that the sons of the Trojans might breathe again from misery,
and destroy the Argives, coming now that you are slain?
For no longer shall there be such courage in them as before,
when they perished in the war; for you were the bulwark against calamity;
nor is the goal of homecoming sweet to me now that you have died here,
but I myself too long to perish in this place,
that with you the life-giving earth may cover me;
for I care not so much for my parents, if anywhere they yet live,
if anywhere they yet dwell about Salamis alive,
as for you who are dead, since you were my glory.”
So he spoke, groaning greatly; and over him groaned divine Tecmessa,
the bedfellow of blameless Ajax, whom, though she was
his captive, he made his own wife, and made her mistress
of all things, of as many as wives in the house,
brought with dowry, manage beside their wedded husbands;
and she, overcome beneath his tireless arms,
bore Eurysaces, a son like in all things to his father;
but he was still a little child, left in his bed;
and she, groaning greatly, fell upon the dear corpse,
flat in the dust, defiling her fair body;
and she cried out a piteous cry, greatly grieving in her heart within:
“Ah me, unhappy that I am, since you are dead, not slain
by the hands of the foe in battle, but by your own self;
so unforgettable grief comes upon me; for I did not hope
to see, when you were slain, the day of many groans
in Troy; but all this the evil Fates have brought to pass;
would that before this the firm earth had gaped for me,
before I saw your pitiless doom; for to me
no other worse calamity ever came into my heart,
not even when first, far from my homeland
and my parents, you dragged me off with the other captive women,
weeping much, since indeed once I was a queen,
revered though I was, and the day of slavery came upon me;
but neither for my pleasant homeland nor for my parents
do I care, now they are gone, so much as for you slain,
because to me, wretched as I was, you devised all that I desired,
and made me your like-minded wife, and said you would
make me at once queen of well-built Salamis
when you returned from Troy; but the god has not brought this to pass for us;
and you are gone from me unseen, nor do you even now
care for me and your child, who shall not delight his heart in his father,
nor mount your throne, but others
shall make him a wretched slave, since when a father is no more
little children are tended by men far
baser; for beneath baneful orphanhood a heavy life
falls to children, and woes pour upon them one from another;
and the day of slavery shall soon come upon me too, wretched,
now that you are gone before, you who were to me as a god.”
When she had so spoken, Agamemnon, kindly minded, addressed her:
“O woman, no other shall ever make you a slave
while blameless Teucer yet lives and I myself;
but we will honour you always with boundless gifts,
we will honour you as a goddess, and your child too, as though
godlike Ajax still lived, who was the strength of the Achaeans.
Would that he had not laid such grief on all Achaea,
slain by his own hand; for not the boundless host
of the foe had strength to slay him in war beneath Ares.”
So he spoke, grieving in his heart within; and about him the people
groaned piteously, and the Hellespont resounded
as they wept, and baleful sorrow spread over them.
And grief seized even wise Odysseus himself
that that man was slain, and grieving in his heart
he spoke this word among the sorrowing Achaeans:
“O friends, how no other evil worse than wrath
ever comes, which breeds for mortals evil strife;
wrath which now too roused mighty Ajax
against me, angered in his heart; would that for me
the sons of the Trojans had never, over the arms of Achilles,
cast the glorious victory, for which, grieving in his heart,
the goodly son of mighty Telamon
perished by his own hands; yet of his wrath I myself am
in no way the cause, but some Fate full of groans, which slew him;
for if my heart within my breast had hoped
that he would so rage in his mind, neither would I
have come contending for the victory, nor would I have let any other
among the Danaans, eager though he was, contend,
but I myself would have taken up the god-given arms
and readily given them to him, even if he longed for aught else besides.
But now I did not think that he, greatly grieving, would be wroth
thereafter, since it was not for a woman
nor for a city that I fought against him, nor for broad wealth,
but my quarrel was for valour, over which strife
is ever sweet to men of good sense;
but that man, noble though he was, by the hateful Fate of a god
erred; for it is not fitting to grieve overmuch in the heart;
for it is the part of a prudent man even amid many sorrows that come upon him
to endure beneath a steadfast heart and firm mind, and not to grieve.”
So spoke the famous son of godlike Laertes.
But when they had had their fill of weeping and grievous sorrow,
then the son of Neleus spoke to them yet grieving:
“O friends, how the Fates with pitiless heart
have swiftly cast upon us grief on grievous grief,
with the death of Ajax and of mighty Achilles
and of other Argives, and of our own son
Antilochus. But it is in no way right to weep for those slain in battle
all our days, and to grieve in the heart,
but to cease from unseemly lament, since it is better
to do what is fitting for mortals over the dead,
a pyre and a tomb, and to bury the bones;
for the dead is in no way roused by laments, nor knows anything
to heed, when the pitiless Fates have closed their jaws about him.”
So he spoke, comforting them; and about him the godlike kings
quickly gathered in a throng, greatly grieving in their hearts within,
and, great though he was, swiftly to the ships they bore him,
many lifting him; and they covered him with cloths,
washing away the blood that about his mighty limbs
lay drying together with his arms and the dust;
and then from the mountains of Ida the young men brought
boundless wood, and on every side they heaped it about the corpse;
and much wood they laid about him, and many sheep
and well-made garments and the glorious herds of oxen,
and horses glorying in their swift feet,
and gleaming gold and the countless arms of warriors,
as many as the glorious man had taken before from the slain,
and upon them clear amber, which they say
is the tear of the daughters of all-prophetic Helios,
which they shed over slain Phaethon,
mourning beside the stream of great Eridanus;
and this Helios, making an imperishable honour for his son,
made amber, a great treasure for men,
which then upon the broad pyre the Argives cast
doing honour to the glorious man fallen,
Ajax; and about him, groaning greatly, they set
precious ivory and lovely silver
and jars of oil and all other things,
as many as adorn glorious and splendid wealth.
And on it they cast the strength of mighty fire; and a breath came
from the sea, which the goddess Thetis sent, that the body
of great Ajax might be consumed; and night and morning
he burned beside the ships, while the wind drove on;
as once before, by the grievous thunderbolt of Zeus,
Enceladus was overcome beneath the tireless sea
below Thrinacia, and the whole island smouldered;
or as Heracles, while yet alive, gave his limbs to the fire to burn,
enraged by the guile of Nessus,
when he dared the great deed, and all Oeta groaned about him
as he burned alive, and his spirit mingled with the air,
leaving the man conspicuous, and he himself was numbered
among the gods, since the earth held his much-toiling body;
so Ajax lay in the fire, forgetful of the war,
with his arms; and a great throng of people thronged
the shores; and the Trojans rejoiced, but the Achaeans grieved.
But when the destroying fire had consumed the goodly body,
then they quenched the pyre with wine; and his bones
they placed in a golden chest; and about them earth
they heaped, boundless, not far from the Rhoetean shore.
And straightway they scattered to the swift-bounding ships,
grieving in spirit; for they honoured him as equal to Achilles.
And black night rushed on, bringing sleep upon men;
and they took their meal and awaited the Dawn-child,
slumbering a little with weary eyelids;
for terribly they feared in their hearts, lest the Trojans
come upon them in the night, now that the son of Telamon was dead.
And Dawn, leaving the stream of Ocean and the bed
of Tithonus, mounted the great heaven, and on every side
she was spread, all-shining; and earth and air laughed;
and mortals turned to their tasks, men who easily perish;
one went to one work, another to another; but the Achaeans
poured into the assembly at the call of Menelaus;
and when at last they were all gathered throughout the host,
then in the midst of them as they gathered he spoke:
“Hear my word, you god-born kings,
as I declare it; for greatly within me my heart is worn
for the perishing of the host, who came for my sake
to the grievous strife, men whom their home shall not receive,
nor their parents; for the Fate of fortune has cut down many.
Would that the heavy strength of unbearable Death
had fallen upon me myself before I gathered the host here;
but now some god has laid unceasing pains upon me,
that I should see many evils; who could rejoice in heart
looking long upon the hopeless works of war?
But come, as many of us as are still left, let us upon the swift ships
flee quickly, each to his own land,
now that Ajax is dead and mighty Achilles,
for I do not think that, when they are slain, we shall escape
destruction, but shall be overcome by the grievous Trojans
for my sake and for that of dog-faced Helen, for whom now
I care nothing, as I care for you, when I behold men slain
in the war; let her go with her most worthless
husband; for a god took her prudent wits
from her heart, when she left my house and my bed.
But these things shall be the care of Priam and the Trojans;
let us at once depart, since it is far better
to flee the ill-sounding war than to perish.”
So he spoke, making trial of the Argives; but other things his heart
pondered within his breast in his jealous spirit,
how he might destroy the Trojans and break the long walls of the city
from their foundations, and glut Ares with much blood
when godlike Alexander had fallen among the slain;
for nothing is more hateful than jealousy.
So he pondered, and sat down upon his seat.
And then the son of Tydeus, the spear-shaker, rose in the midst,
and quickly rebuked Menelaus dear to Ares:
“Ah, wretched son of Atreus, why now does grievous fear
seize you, and you speak such things among the Argives,
like a child or a woman, whose strength is feeble?
But the best sons of the Achaeans will not obey you
before they cast all the battlements of Troy to the ground;
for courage is great glory to men, but flight a reproach.
And if any of these too obeys, as you bid,
at once will I cut off his head with the dark iron,
and cast him to the high-flying birds for food.
But come, you whose care it is to rouse the spirit of men,
let them at once urge on all the host along the ships
to whet their spears, and set the shields beside them and all else
in good order, and let all at once take their meal,
both men and horses that are eager for war;
and on the plain Ares will most swiftly decide.”
So spoke the son of Tydeus, and sat down where he had been before;
and to them the son of Thestor spoke this word,
standing up in the midst, where it is right to speak in assembly:
“Hear me, dear children of the war-abiding Argives;
for you know how clearly I am skilled to declare oracles.
Already before this I said that in the tenth year
we should sack steep Ilium; and that now the immortals
are bringing to pass; and victory lies at the feet of the Achaeans.
But come, let us send the son of Tydeus and steadfast Odysseus
swiftly to Scyros in a black ship,
who by persuasion shall bring the mighty son
of Achilles; and a great light he shall bring to us all.”
So spoke the son of wise Thestor; and about him the host
shouted in gladness, since their hearts hoped
that the word of Calchas was true, as he spoke;
and then the son of Laertes spoke among the Achaeans:
“O friends, it is no longer fitting to say much among you
this day; for there is weariness now upon men in grief;
for I know that to a weary host neither a speaker
is pleasing, nor a singer, whom the immortal Pierides
love; men have desire then for few words.
Now then, that which has pleased all throughout the Argive host,
with the son of Tydeus most of all going with me, I would accomplish;
for we two going will bring the mighty son
of war-loving Achilles, persuading him with words,
even if his mother greatly lamenting holds him back
in the halls; for I hope in my heart that the son
of a mighty father is warlike.”
When he had so spoken, prudent Menelaus addressed him:
“O Odysseus, great help of the mighty Argives,
if indeed the mighty son of great-souled Achilles
should come at your persuasion as a helper to us who long for it
from Scyros, and if some one of the heavenly ones grants
victory to us who pray, and I reach the land of Hellas,
I will give him my glorious daughter for a wife,
Hermione, and many rich gifts with her
freely; for I think he will neither scorn his wife
nor his noble father-in-law overweeningly.”
So he spoke; and the Danaans assented with their words.
And then the assembly broke up; and they scattered to the ships,
eager for their meal, which is strength for men;
and when they had ceased, sated with abundant food,
then together with wise Odysseus the son of Tydeus
drew a swift ship into the boundless sea;
and quickly they went in, and stowed all the gear;
and they themselves went aboard; and with them twenty men
skilled in rowing, both when the winds blow against them
and when calm spreads beneath the wide sea.
And when they had sat at the well-made benches,
they struck the great wave of the sea; and much foam seethed about;
and the watery paths were cut through about the oars
as the ship sped on; and they sweated as they rowed;
as when beneath the yokes oxen greatly wearied
drag the wooden wagon forward, eager,
groaning beneath the burden upon the whirling axle,
worn down, while much sweat down their necks and shoulders
for both runs down to the ground;
so then the young men toiled at the sturdy oars;
and very swiftly they crossed the wide sea.
But the other Achaeans watched them as they went;
and they whetted the dread arrows and spears with which they fought.
But the Trojans within the city, undaunted, made ready
eager for the war, and praying to the blessed gods
for a rest from slaughter and a breathing-space from toil.
And to them as they longed for it the gods brought a great bulwark against calamity,
Eurypylus, of the line of mighty Heracles;
and the host followed him, men skilled in battle,
many, all who dwelt by the streams of long Caïcus,
trusting in their strong spears.
And about him the sons of the Trojans greatly rejoiced in their hearts;
as when, penned within an enclosure, tame geese behold
a man who casts food to them,
and about him standing in a circle they cackle with their bills,
and fawn, and his heart is warmed as he looks on;
so the sons of the Trojans rejoiced when they beheld
mighty Eurypylus, and his bold heart within him
took delight in those who gathered; and from the porches the women
marvelled at the godlike man; and he sped forth conspicuous among the host
like a lion that has come down among the jackals in the mountains.
And Paris welcomed him, and honoured him as equal to Hector;
for he was his cousin, sprung of one stock;
for him the divine sister of Priam bore,
Astyoche, mingling beneath the strong arms
of Telephus, whom indeed to fearless Heracles,
in secret from her father, fair-haired Auge bore;
and him, while still a babe craving the breast,
once a swift hind reared, and loved him like her own fawn,
offering her teat by the will of Zeus; for it was not fitting
that the offspring of Heracles should miserably perish.
And his glorious son Paris with right willing heart
led to his own house through the spacious city,
past the tomb of Assaracus and the lofty halls of Hector
and the most holy temple of the Tritonian, where near at hand
were his dwellings and the pure altar of Zeus of the Court;
and of his brothers and kinsmen and his parents
he asked him eagerly; and the other told him all;
and both, conversing thus, went on together.
And they came to the great and wealthy house; there sat
godlike Helen, clothed in the beauty of the Graces;
and about her four handmaids busily moved,
and others apart, away from the famous chamber,
were busy with such works as befit servants.
And Helen greatly marvelled, looking upon Eurypylus,
and he in turn at Helen; and they greeted one another
with words in the fragrant house;
and the servants set two thrones near the queen;
and straightway Alexander sat down, and beside him
Eurypylus. And the host before the city made their camp
where the strong-souled watchmen of the Trojans were;
and quickly they set their arms upon the ground, and beside them the horses
they stood, still panting from their wretched toil;
and they cast before them in the mangers what the swift horses eat.
And then night rushed on, and earth and air grew dark;
and they took their meal before the lofty wall,
the Ceteians and the Trojans; and much talk arose
as they feasted; and everywhere the strength of smoky fire
blazed beside the huts; and the shrill pipe sounded
and flutes fitted with clear-toned reeds,
and about them rose the lovely cry of the lyres.
And the Argives afar off marvelled, looking on
upon the many fires on the plain, and hearing the boundless
cry of flutes and lyres and of men and horses
and of the pipe, which is conspicuous at the feast and among herdsmen;
therefore each one in his own huts gave command
to guard the ships by turns until dawn,
lest the proud Trojans should come and burn them,
they who then before the lofty wall were feasting.
And likewise in the house of Alexander the warlike
son of Telephus feasted among the glorious kings;
and much both Priam and the other sons of the Trojans
in turn prayed that he would close with the Argives
in the grievous hour; and he promised to accomplish all.
But when they had supped, they went each to his own house;
and Eurypylus lay down there a little apart
in a well-built chamber, where before noble Alexander
himself was wont to sleep beside his glorious wife;
for that was the most splendid and far the best of all;
there he went and lay; and the rest took their rest elsewhere
until fair-throned Dawn. But with the dawn
the son of Telephus rose up and came to the wide host
with the other kings, all who were about Ilium;
and the host straightway sank into their arms, eager,
all longing to toil among the foremost;
and so too Eurypylus set about his great limbs
arms like to gleaming lightnings;
and on his divine shield lay much cunning work,
all that the bold strength of Heracles had wrought before.
There were two serpents, licking with grim jaws,
like to things in motion, in their dart,
straining horribly; but he, one here, one there,
though but a babe, was overcoming them; and his heart
was fearless, and his spirit, since he was like Zeus in strength
from the beginning; for no race of the heavenly gods
is fruitless or helpless, but might
attended him, boundless, even when he was within the womb.
There too was wrought the strength of the Nemean lion,
beneath the sturdy hands of mighty Heracles
grievously crushed; and about his grim jaws
there was bloody foam; and he seemed to be gasping out his life.
Near it laboured the strength of the many-necked hydra,
licking terribly; and her painful heads,
some had been laid low upon the ground, but others grew up,
many from few; and toil held Heracles
and bold Iolaus, since both thought strong thoughts,
the one cutting off the raging heads
with the crooked-toothed sickle swiftly, the other burning with iron
set ablaze; and the strong onset of the beast was overcome.
Next was wrought the strength of the tireless boar
foaming at the jaws; and he bore it, as though in truth,
alive to Eurystheus, the great strength of Alcides.
And the hind was well wrought, swift of foot, which over the lands
of grievous dwellers round about greatly ravaged every field;
and her, by the golden horn, the mighty hero
held fast, breathing the breath of deadly fire.
And about were the hateful Stymphalian birds; some, struck
by arrows, gasped out their life in the dust, and others, still mindful
of flight, sped through the gray air;
and at them Heracles, enraged, one after another
ever sent an arrow, like one greatly hastening.
There too was the great steading of godlike Augeas
cunningly wrought upon the tireless oxhide;
and to it the deep stream of the divine Alpheus
mighty Heracles led on; and about him the Nymphs
marvelled at the boundless work. And far off was the bull
fire-breathing, which, mighty though it was,
he bent by force of its strong horn; and the tireless
sinews of both were strained as he pressed upon it;
and it seemed to send forth a bellowing. And near it,
about the shield, was wrought, clothed in the form of the goddesses,
Hippolyte; and her, beneath his strong hands,
eager to strip her of her cunning belt,
he seized by the hair as she rode the swift horse; and apart
the other Amazons trembled. And about were the deadly
man-eating mares of Diomedes throughout the Thracian land;
and these at the hateful mangers,
together with the king who plotted evil, he slew.
There too was the body of tireless Geryon
lying dead among his cattle; and his heads in the dust
lay bloody, overcome by the force of the club;
and before him lay slain the dog most deadly of all,
Orthrus, like in his mighty strength to grievous
Cerberus, who was his brother; and beside lay
the herdsman Eurytion, defiled with much blood.
And about it were wrought the golden apples gleaming
of the Hesperides upon the undefiled tree-trunk; and about it
a terrible serpent lay slain; and they, one here, one there,
cowering, fled the bold son of great Zeus.
There too was a great terror even for the immortals to behold,
Cerberus, whom to tireless Typhoeus Echidna bore
in a chill cave near black grievous Night;
and he was a monstrous and hideous thing,
before the deadly gates of much-bewailed Hades
keeping back the throng of the dead beneath the misty pit;
and easily the son of Zeus, mastering him with blows,
led him heavy-headed past the steep streams of Styx,
dragging him unwilling by force to an unwonted place
boldly. And far off were wrought the long glens
of Caucasus; and the bonds of Prometheus, this way and that,
together with the very rocks to which they were fitted,
he broke and loosed the great Titan; and grievous beside him lay
the eagle, its body struck with a painful arrow.
And there was wrought the great strength of the mighty Centaurs
about the hall of Pholus; strife and wine roused them
to fight against Heracles, those monsters;
and some lay slain about the pine-trunks
which they held in their hands as a remedy of battle; but others still
fought with the long firs, eager, nor did they cease
from the conflict; and the heads of all were wet with gore
as they were struck in the pitiless strife, as though in truth;
and blood was mingled with wine, and all was crushed together,
the food and the mixing-bowls and the well-polished tables.
And Nessus, on the other side, by the stream of Evenus,
who had escaped from that battle, he overcame with an arrow,
enraged about his lovely wife; and there too was wrought
the great strength of mighty Antaeus, whom likewise,
as he strove fiercely about the wrestling,
he lifted high and crushed with his strong hands.
And at the mouths of fair-flowing Hellespont lay
a grievous great sea-monster, struck by pitiless arrows;
and he loosed Hesione from her cruel bonds.
And other countless deeds of bold-hearted Alcides
the wide shield of god-nurtured Eurypylus held about it.
And he seemed like Ares as he rushed among the ranks;
and the Trojans about him rejoiced when they beheld
both the arms and the man, clothed in the form of the gods;
and Paris, urging him to battle, addressed him:
“I rejoice that you have come, since now my heart hopes
that all the Argives will miserably perish
together with their ships, since never such a mortal
have I seen among the Trojans or among the warlike Achaeans.
But come, by great and mighty Heracles,
whom in size and strength and splendid form you resemble,
remembering him and devising deeds worthy of him,
boldly defend the Trojans as they are slaughtered,
that we may somehow breathe again; for you alone I think
can ward off the evil dooms from the perishing city.”
So he spoke, greatly urging; and the other addressed him with words:
“Great-souled son of Priam, in form like the blessed ones,
these things are fixed upon the knees of the immortals,
whether one dies in the violent battle or is saved;
but we, as is fitting and as we have strength to fight,
will stand before the city; and this too I will swear,
that I will not turn back before I either slay or perish.”
So he spoke boldly; and the Trojans rejoiced greatly.
And then Alexander and high-souled Aeneas
and Polydamas of the good ash-spear and noble Pammon
and Deïphobus after them and Aethicus, who above all
the Paphlagonians was foremost to endure the throng in battle,
all these he chose together, men who knew how to toil,
that against the foremost foes they might fight
in the war; and very quickly they went before the host;
and eagerly they sped from the city; and about them many
of the host followed, as when the famous tribes of bees
pour after their leaders from the covered hive
with a buzzing, when the day of spring comes;
so the men followed them as they went to battle;
and of them as they came a great din reached the air,
of themselves and of their horses; and the boundless arms rang about.
And as when the strength of a great wind, leaping forth,
stirs from the roots the depth of the barren sea,
and the dark waves swiftly roaring toward the shores
spit out the seaweed as the surge belches it,
and a din rises along the barren beaches;
so beneath the rush of these the monstrous earth resounded.
And the Argives apart before the wall poured forth
about godlike Agamemnon; and there rose a cry of the host
calling upon one another to face the deadly war
and not to cower at the rebuke
and stay beside the ships, eager as they were to fight.
And they met the rushing Trojans, as when calves
from the thicket meet the cattle coming to the steading
from the spring pasture down the mountain, when the fields
bloom thick, and the earth teems with flowers,
and the bowls are full again with the milk of cattle and of sheep,
and a great lowing rises here and there
as they mingle, and the herdsman rejoices among them;
so, as these rushed against one another, an uproar
arose; for terribly they shouted on both sides.
They stretched out the boundless battle; and Tumult
turned among them with grievous Slaughter;
and shields and spears and helmets fell together
close by; and the bronze flashed like fire all about;
and the battle bristled with spears; and on every side with blood
the black earth was wet as the heroes were slain
and the swift-footed horses, which were poured about the chariots,
some still gasping beneath the axles, others
falling from above; and a hateful cry rushed through the air;
for brazen strife had fallen upon both sides;
and some fought with cruel stones,
others with new-edged javelins and arrows,
others with axes and double-edged battle-axes
and strong swords and close-fighting spears,
each holding in his hands some defence of battle.
First the Argives thrust back the Trojan ranks
a little from themselves; but they, rushing back again,
wet Ares with blood, leaping among the Argives;
and Eurypylus among them, like a black hurricane,
went against all the host and slew the Argives
boldly; for Zeus granted him boundless might,
showing favour to glorious Heracles.
There he struck Nireus too, a man like to the gods,
as he fought the Trojans, with his long spear
a little above the navel; and he fell to the ground of earth;
and the blood gushed from him, and his glorious arms were wet,
and his splendid form was wet together with his flourishing hair;
and he lay in the dust and blood among the slain,
like a flourishing shoot of a well-cleft olive,
which the force of a river along its roaring stream
with its banks drives down, when it has rent the whole channel
from the roots, and it lies heavy with its blossoms;
so then upon the boundless ground of earth Nireus' goodly
body was poured out, and his lovely splendour;
and over him, slain, Eurypylus greatly boasted:
“Lie now in the dust, since your admired beauty
in no way availed you, much as you longed for it, but I
have robbed you of life, much as you longed to escape;
wretch, you did not see that you came against a better man;
for beauty is no match for strength in the press of battle.”
So speaking, he set about taking the famous arms of the slain,
rushing on; but against him came Machaon
enraged for Nireus, whose fate he had endured close beside;
and with his grievous spear he struck him across the broad shoulder,
the right one, and the blood gushed, mighty though he was;
yet not even so did he draw back from the cruel tumult,
but like a lion or a wild boar in the mountains
he raged in the midst, that he might overcome him who came on,
him who first wounded him, darting ahead through the throng;
this purposing he rushed upon Machaon, and quickly
wounded him with his spear, long and sturdy,
on the right buttock; but the other did not draw back,
nor did he avoid the onset, though the blood gushed;
but quickly raising a huge stone
he cast it at the head of great-souled Telephus' son;
but his helmet warded off grievous slaughter and woe
swiftly; and then more was he wroth with the strong man,
Eurypylus, and greatly grieving in his spirit
he swiftly drove his spear through the breast of Machaon.
And the bloody point reached even to his back;
and he fell as when a bull beneath the jaws of a lion;
and about his limbs his gleaming arms rang loudly.
And Eurypylus straightway drew out the grievous point
from the flesh of the wounded man, and boasting greatly cried out:
“Ah wretch, your heart was not at all well fitted in your wits,
you who, though a man of no account, against a far better man
came face to face; therefore an evil Fate of fortune fell upon you.
But this shall be your gain, when the birds devour
your flesh, slain in the battle; or do you still hope
to return home and escape my might and my hands?
You are a healer, and you know full well soothing remedies,
trusting in which you hoped perhaps to escape the evil day.
But not even your father himself from windy Olympus
shall save your heart from death,
not even if he pour nectar and ambrosia upon you.”
So he spoke; and breathing faintly the other addressed him:
“Eurypylus, for you too it is not fated to live
for a long time, but close beside you stands deadly Doom
over the Trojan plain, you who now speak insolent things.”
When he had so spoken, his spirit left him; and he went at once within Hades;
and even now that he was no more the glorious man addressed him:
“Now then lie there beneath the earth; but I
care not for the hereafter, even if soon gentle to my feet
the grievous destruction comes this day; for in no way do men
live forever; doom is appointed for all.”
So speaking he wounded the corpse; and greatly Teucer cried out
when he saw Machaon in the dust; for afar off
he was standing, toiling hard; for there in the midst
lay the strife; and one onset rose upon another.
Yet not even so did he neglect the noble man fallen,
Nireus, who lay close beside; but he saw him
later amid the dust of godlike Machaon;
and at once he called to the Argives, shouting aloud:
“Rush on, Argives, and yield not to the rushing
foes; for boundless shall be our reproach,
if divine Machaon together with godlike Nireus
the Trojans drag off and bear back to Ilium.
But come, let us fight the foe with willing heart,
that we may either drag off the slain, or ourselves
die beside them, since this is the right of men,
to defend their own, and not to leave them a prey to others;
for not without sweat does glory grow among men.”
So he spoke; and grief came upon the Danaans; and about them
many reddened the earth, slain beneath Ares,
as they fought on either side; and an equal strife arose.
At last Podalirius perceived the grievous slaughter
of his brother, struck down in the dust, for by the swift ships
he sat tending the wounds of men struck by spears,
healing them. And he put on all his arms,
enraged in spirit for his brother; and in him valour
terribly grew within his breast as he raged
to the grievous war; and his dark blood seethed,
fierce, beneath his heart; and swiftly he leapt among the foes,
brandishing in his swift hands a long-pointed javelin;
and quickly he took the noble son of Agamestor,
Clitus, whom a fair-haired Nymph bore about the streams
of Parthenius, which flows through the land like oil,
pouring its fair-flowing water into the Euxine sea.
And another he slew, a foeman, about his brother,
Lassus, whom godlike Pronoe bore about the streams
of the river Nymphaeus very near the wide cave,
the wondrous cave, which men say is of them,
the sacred cave of the Nymphs, all who dwell about the long
mountains of the Paphlagonians, and all who dwell about clustered
Heraclea; and that cave is like the work of the gods,
for it is wrought boundless to behold,
of stone, and cold water goes through the cavern,
like crystal, and in its innermost recesses everywhere
stone mixing-bowls upon the hard rocks
appear as though made by the hands of men;
and about them are Pans together with lovely Nymphs,
and looms and distaffs, and all such cunning
works as belong to mortals, which appear a marvel
to men coming within the sacred recess;
in it are two descents and ways up,
the one turned toward the resounding north
wind, the other facing the south that blows moist,
by which mortals pass beneath the wide cave of the goddesses;
but the other is the road of the blessed, nor do men
easily tread it, since a wide chasm is wrought
down to the pit of high-souled Aïdoneus;
but these things it is the right of the blessed to behold.
About Machaon and the glorious son of Aglaïe,
as men fought on either side, a great throng perished;
at last the Danaans dragged them away, after much
labour; and quickly to their own ships they carried them,
a few, since upon the greater part wretched misery
of the grievous war was spread; and they remained in toil by necessity.
But when very many had filled up the dark dooms
amid the bloody and grievous tumult,
then many of the Argives fled within the ships,
as many as Eurypylus pressed hard upon, rolling great calamity.
A few about Ajax and the two mighty sons of Atreus
remained in the battle; and soon all would have perished
by the hands of the foes as they turned about in the throng,
had not the son of Oïleus struck wise Polydamas
with his spear by the left shoulder near the breast;
and the blood gushed from him; and he drew back a little.
And far-famed Menelaus wounded Deïphobus
by the right breast; but he escaped on swift feet.
Then godlike Agamemnon slew a great throng
from the deadly multitude; and after noble Aethicus he went
raging with his spear; but the other fled among his comrades.
But when host-rousing Eurypylus perceived them
all drawing back together from the hateful tumult,
at once he left the host, as many as he was driving toward the ships,
and swiftly rushed upon the two mighty sons of Atreus
and the strong-hearted son of Oïleus, who in running
was swift, and in battle was foremost.
Upon them he rushed swiftly, holding his long spear;
and with him came Paris and high-souled Aeneas,
who swiftly struck Ajax with a long stone
upon his strong helmet; but he, stretched in the dust,
breathed not out his life, since for him the fated day
was appointed in his homecoming about the Capherean rocks;
and his comrades dear to Ares snatched him up,
still faintly breathing, and bore him to the ships of the Achaeans.
And then the glorious kings were left alone,
the sons of Atreus; and about them stood a deadly throng
casting from either side whatever their hands had strength to take;
for some poured grievous arrows, others stones,
others javelins; and they, being in the midst,
turned about, like boars within an enclosure, or lions
on the day when lords gather men together
and grievously hem them in, devising evil destruction
for the strong beasts, while these, within the enclosure,
tear the servants, whoever comes near them;
so they in the midst slew those who rushed upon them.
Yet not even so had they strength, though they longed, to escape,
had not Teucer come, and high-souled Idomeneus,
and Meriones and Thoas and godlike Thrasymedes,
who before feared the bold strength of Eurypylus,
and would have fled to the ships, avoiding the heavy calamity,
had they not, fearing greatly for the sons of Atreus, come
face to face with Eurypylus; and a baleful battle arose.
Then Teucer of the good ash-spear thrust his spear
against the shield of Aeneas; but he wounded not his fair flesh;
for the great fourfold ox-hide shield warded off the calamity;
but even so, afraid, he drew back a little.
And Meriones rushed upon blameless Laophoön,
son of Paeon, whom fair-haired Cleomede bore
by the streams of Axius; and he came to holy Ilium
to aid the Trojans with blameless Asteropaeus;
him Meriones pierced with his jagged spear
above the privy parts; and swiftly the point drew out
his bowels; and most swiftly his spirit sped to the darkness.
And Ajax' comrade, the warlike son of Oïleus,
Alcimedes, cast into the throng of the mighty Trojans;
and praying he hurled into the dread battle-cry of the foes
a grievous stone from his sling; and the men trembled through
at the whir and at the stone, fearing greatly as it came.
And deadly Fate bore it to the bold charioteer
of Pammon, the son of Hippasus; and as he held the reins in his hands
it struck him upon the temple; and swiftly it cast him from the chariot
before his own wheel; and the swift car of him as he fell
rolled his wretched body back beneath the wheel-rims
as the horses sped on; and dread death overcame him
swiftly, leaving whip and reins behind;
and grief fell upon Pammon; and at once necessity made him
both king and charioteer of the swift car;
and now would he have endured there his doom and his last day,
had not some Trojan, in the bloody tumult,
taken the reins in his hands and saved the king
already hard pressed by the deadly hands of the foes.
And godlike Acamas, rushing against him,
the mighty son of Nestor struck above the knee with his spear;
and into the deadly wound there entered hateful pains;
and he drew back from the war; and he left to his comrades the tumult
full of tears; for war was no longer his care.
And then the squire of glorious Eurypylus
struck Thoas' comrade Echemmon in the battle
a little below the shoulder; and about his heart the spear
came, grievous; and with the blood there oozed sweat
cold from his limbs; and as he turned to be borne
back, the great strength of Eurypylus caught him;
and cut his swift sinews; and his feet against his will stayed
there, where he struck him; and the immortal life left him.
Swiftly Thoas pierced Paris with his sharp spear
on the right thigh; and he went back a little
to fetch his swift bow, which he had left behind.
And Idomeneus, raising a stone with his hands, as much as he had strength for,
cast it upon the arm of Eurypylus; and to the ground
his deadly spear fell; and at once he drew back
to fetch his spear; for the one he had he let fall from his hand.
And the sons of Atreus breathed a little from the war.
But swiftly his squires came near him, who brought him
an unbreakable long spear, which loosed the knees of many;
and taking it he went against the host, raging in his might,
slaying whomever he met, and overcoming a great throng.
Then neither did the sons of Atreus stand firm nor any other
of the close-fighting Danaans; for grievous fear seized them all;
for upon all rushed calamity, arming itself,
Eurypylus; and following behind he made havoc.
And he called out again to the Trojans and his horse-taming comrades:
“O friends, come, take courage in your breasts
and work for the Danaans slaughter and unseen doom,
they who now like sheep are departing
to their own ships; but let us all remember
the deadly battle, in which from childhood we are skilled.”
So he spoke; and they rushed in a throng upon the Argives;
and they, trembling greatly, fled from the grievous tumult;
and the others followed like white-toothed dogs
upon wild hinds along the long glens and the wood.
And many they cast in the dust, eager though they were
to escape the grievous war-cry of deadly slaughter.
Eurypylus slew blameless Bucolion
and Nesus and Chromius and Antiphus; and they dwelt
in wealthy Mycene, while the others dwelt in Lacedaemon;
these he slew, well known though they were.
And out of the multitude he took countless tribes of men,
as many as I have no strength to sing, though I long to,
not even if there were a heart of iron in my breast.
And Aeneas slew Pheres and Antimachus,
both of whom had come from Crete with Idomeneus.
And noble Agenor slew blameless Molus,
who came from Argos under king Sthenelus;
him he struck with a new-whetted javelin far behind
as he fled from the war, hitting him beneath the lowest part of his right
shin; and the point cut clean through the broad sinew,
driving straight on; and it grievously sheared the bones of the man
beside; and death was mingled with pain, and the man perished.
Then Paris struck Mosynus and brave Phorcys,
both brothers, who came from Salamis
in the ships of Ajax, and saw their homecoming no more.
Upon them he took Cleolaus, the goodly squire of Meges,
striking him on the left breast; and about him night,
evil, seized, and his spirit flew away; and as he was overcome,
within, beneath his breast, his grievous heart
beating fast still made the feathered shaft quiver.
And he sent another arrow at bold Eëtion
swiftly; and at once through his jaw it passed,
the bronze; and he groaned; and with his blood mingled his tear.
And one slew another; and a great space was crowded
with the Argives fallen in heaps upon one another.
And now would the Trojans have burned the ships with fire,
had not night rushed on, bringing deep-shadowed darkness.
And Eurypylus drew back, and with him the other sons of the Trojans
a little apart from the ships toward the mouths of Simoeis,
where they made their camp rejoicing. But among the ships
the Argives lamented, falling upon the sands,
grieving greatly for the slain, because of them
black doom had overtaken many in the dust.
And when heaven hid the stars, and Dawn awoke
shining bright, and the darkness of night drew back,
then the warlike sons of the mighty Argives,
some went before the ships to the strong battle
eager to face Eurypylus, while others apart,
there beside the ships, gave burial to Machaon
and Nireus, who was like the everliving blessed ones
in beauty and splendour; but in might he was not strong;
for the gods do not grant all things together to men,
but close beside the noble man some evil stands, from some fate;
so for king Nireus, beside his lovely splendour,
lay feebleness; yet the Danaans did not neglect him,
but gave him burial and mourned over the tomb
as much as they did divine Machaon, whom equal to the immortal gods
they ever honoured, since he knew close-packed counsels;
and quickly they raised one mound about them both.
And then on the plain deadly Ares still raged;
and on both sides rose a great din and a cry
as the ox-hide shields were shattered by stones and spears;
and they toiled beneath much-laborious Ares;
but unceasingly, without taste of food, in the dust
lay Podalirius, groaning greatly; nor did he leave
the tomb of his brother; and his mind was set
to perish pitilessly by his own hands.
And now he laid his hands upon his sword, and now again
he sought a dread drug; but his comrades held him back,
much comforting him; yet he ceased not from his grief.
And now he would have lost his life by his own hands
at the new-made tomb of his noble brother,
had not the son of Neleus heard him, and not neglected him
as he was sorely worn; and he found him now perhaps
poured out about the much-bewailed tomb, and now again
pouring dust about his head, and beating his breast
with strong hands, and calling by name
on his brother; and the servants together with his comrades
groaned about their lord; and evil misery held them all.
And he addressed him in his great grief with gentle words:
“Cease from grievous wailing and dread sorrow,
O child; for it is not fitting that a man born wise
should mourn like a woman, falling upon one who is no more;
for you will not raise him again into the light, since unseen
his soul has flown to the air, and his body apart
the deadly fire devoured, and the earth received his bones;
and even as he flourished, so he has perished. Endure your grief
unspeakable, as I too, having lost a son not at all worse
than Machaon, beneath the hands of the foes, a son well skilled
with the javelin and well adorned with prudence. Nor did any other
of the young men love his father as that one loved me,
and he died for my sake, eager to save
his father; yet at once, though he was slain, I had the heart
to taste food, and to look while still alive upon the Dawn-child,
knowing well that all of us men go down the same road
of Hades, and that for all there lie appointed the grievous
bounds of the doom of groans. It befits a mortal man
to bear all things, both the good a god gives and the grievous.”
So he spoke; and grieving the other answered him; and grievous
the tear still ran down and wet his splendid cheeks:
“O father, unbearable grief overcomes my heart
for my wise brother, who reared me
when our father had gone to heaven, like his own son
in his own arms, and the healing of diseases
taught me from his heart; and at one feast and one bed
we took our delight, gladdened by shared possessions;
therefore unforgettable grief comes upon me; nor any more,
now that he is dead, do I long to look upon the goodly light.”
So he spoke; and the old man addressed him in his grief:
“To all men alike a god has given one evil,
bereavement, and the earth shall cover all of us too,
though we do not accomplish the same road of life,
nor such a road as each man desires, since from above
things good and bad lie upon the knees of the gods,
countless, all mingled into one; and these no one
of the immortals sees, but they are made invisible,
veiled in a divine mist; and upon them only Fate
lays her hands, and not seeing, from Olympus
sends them down to earth; and they are borne this way and that
like the blasts of the wind; and often upon a noble man
great trouble is poured, and upon a wretch fortune falls
unfitting. Blind is the life of man;
and therefore he goes not securely, but with his feet
often stumbles; and his shifting path turns
now toward much-groaning trouble, and now again
toward good; and no mortal is made wholly fortunate
from beginning to end; one thing and another meet each man.
It does not become us, who live but a little while, to live
amid griefs. Hope always for better things, and set not
your heart upon sorrow; for indeed there is a saying among men
that the souls of the good go ever to imperishable heaven,
but those of the grievous toward the darkness; and both these
belonged to your brother; for he was both gentle to mortals
and the son of an immortal; and I think that to the race
of the gods he has gone up, by the counsels of his own father.”
So speaking he raised him from the ground, unwilling,
winning him with words, and led him from the dread tomb,
as he kept turning back and still groaning grievously;
and they came to the ships; and the other Achaeans had grievous
toil, and the Trojans, as the war was stirred.
And Eurypylus, with a heart untiring, a match for Ares,
with tireless hands and raging spear
overcame the hostile tribes; and the earth was crowded with the dead
slain on either side. And he, treading among the corpses,
fought boldly, his hands and feet defiled
with blood; nor did he cease from the cruel tumult;
but he overcame strong-hearted Peneleos with his spear
as he faced him in the pitiless strife; and about him many
he slew; nor did he turn his hands from the battle,
but followed the Argives, enraged, as once before
mighty Heracles upon the long heights of Pholoe
rushed upon the Centaurs, raging in his great strength,
and slew them all together, swift though they were
and strong and skilled in deadly war;
so he, one upon another, the host of Danaan spearmen
overcame, rushing on; and they in throngs, one here, one there,
fell in heaps and poured out in the dust.
And as when a boundless river bears down,
and the banks are sheared away in a sandy place,
countless on either side, and it rushes into the swell of the sea
seething along its grievous stream, and on every side
the cliffs resound, and the long channels roar
as they ever crumble, and all the dikes yield to it;
so the glorious sons of the warlike Argives,
many, beneath Eurypylus fell down in the dust,
whomever he overtook in the bloody battle; but they escaped,
as many as the strength of their feet saved; yet even so
they dragged Peneleos out of the ill-sounding throng
to their own ships, though with swift feet
they fled the hateful dooms and pitiless doom.
In full rout they fled within the ships; nor in heart
had they strength to contend against Eurypylus,
because Heracles had sent grievous flight upon them,
exalting his tireless grandson to the utmost.
And they, within the wall, cowering, remained,
like goats that beneath a headland flee a dread blast
which brings much snow and chill hail,
rushing on cold; and they, eager though they are for pasture,
because of the gust do not look straight over the hill,
but wait out the storm beneath shelter and in the ravines
gathered, and beneath the shady bushes they graze
in throngs, until the evil blasts of the wind cease;
so the Danaans remained beneath their own towers,
trembling at the mighty son of Telephus as he rushed upon them.
And he would have destroyed the swift ships and the host,
had not Tritogeneia at last cast courage upon the Argives,
late though it was; and they, ceaselessly, from the lofty wall
casting at the foes with grievous shafts,
slew them one after another; and the walls were wet with grievous
gore; and there was groaning of slaughtered men.
And thus by night and by day they fought,
the Ceteians and the Trojans and the war-abiding Argives,
now before the ships, now about the lofty
wall, since the toil was unbearable; yet even so
for two days they ceased from slaughter and grievous battle,
because to king Eurypylus there came
a message from the Danaans, that, leaving off from war,
they might give to the pyre those slain in the fight;
and he at once assented, and, ceasing from the grievous tumult,
on both sides they buried the dead
fallen in the dust; and the Achaeans above all
mourned Peneleos; and they cast upon the dead man a tomb
very broad and high and conspicuous to those to come;
and the multitude of slain heroes apart
they buried, grieving in heart with great sorrow,
heaping up one pyre for all together
and a grave. And so too apart the sons of the Trojans
buried their slain. And deadly Strife did not cease,
but still urged on the bold strength of Eurypylus
to face the foes; and he did not yet draw back from the ships,
but remained, raising evil battle against the Danaans.
And they came to Scyros, speeding in their black ship;
and they found the son of Achilles before his own house,
now casting with arrows and spears,
now again toiling with his swift-footed horses;
and they rejoiced to see him going about the works
of cruel war, though greatly worn in heart
for his slain father; for that he had learned before.
And quickly they came toward him in awe, because they saw him
in form most fair, like to bold Achilles;
and forestalling them he spoke this word:
“O strangers, greatly I greet you who come to my house;
tell me whence you are and who you are, and what need
brings you to me over the barren swell.”
So he spoke, asking; and godlike Odysseus answered him:
“We are friends of warlike Achilles,
to whom they say wise Deidameia bore you;
and we ourselves liken your form to that man
wholly; and he was like the mighty immortals.
I am from Ithaca, and he from horse-pasturing Argos,
if ever you heard the name of warlike Tydeus' son,
or of shrewd Odysseus, who now near you
stands, I myself, having come for the sake of an oracle;
but have pity quickly, and aid the Argives,
coming to Troy; for so shall there be an end to the war.
And the noble Achaeans will give you boundless gifts;
and the arms of your godlike father I myself
will give you, which wearing you shall greatly rejoice; for they are not
like the arms of mortals, but seem rather equal
to the weapons of the god Ares; and much gold,
adorned with cunning work, is fitted all about them,
with which even Hephaestus himself greatly gladdened
his heart among the immortals as he fashioned
those immortal arms, which will be a great marvel to you
to behold, since earth and heaven and sea
are wrought about the shield, and in its boundless circle
living things are fashioned round, like things in motion,
a marvel even to the immortals; and never such things
has any mortal beheld before among men, nor worn,
except your father, whom equal to Zeus all the Achaeans
honoured, and I most of all, loving him with right good heart;
and when he was slain I bore his body to the ships,
dealing pitiless doom to many foes;
therefore his glorious arms were given me
by divine Thetis; and these, much as I long for them,
I will give you freely, when you come to Ilium.
And Menelaus too, when we have sacked the city of Priam
and returned with our ships to Hellas,
will at once make you his son-in-law, if you wish,
for your good service; and he will give you boundless wealth
to take, possessions and gold, with his fair-haired daughter,
as much as befits a wealthy king to bestow.”
When he had so spoken, the mighty son of Achilles addressed him:
“If indeed the Achaeans by oracles call me,
tomorrow let us go at once over the wide depths of the sea,
that I may be some light to the Danaans who long for it;
but now let us go to my house and the hospitable table,
such as it is right to prepare for strangers;
and concerning my marriage the gods hereafter will care.”
So speaking he led the way; and they followed, greatly rejoicing;
and when they came to the great house and the fair court,
they found Deidameia grieving in her heart
and wasting away, as snow melts upon the mountains
beneath the shrill east wind and the unwearied sun;
so she pined for her noble husband fallen;
and the glorious kings, grieving though she was, greeted her
with words; and her son, coming near to her,
told her truly the lineage and name of each;
but the need for which he had come he hid until dawn,
lest tearful grief should seize her in her sorrow,
and she, much entreating, hold him back as he hastened away.
And quickly they took their meal and gladdened their hearts with sleep,
all who dwelt about the land of sea-girt Scyros,
about which the waves of the long sea roar loud
as they break upon the Aegean shores;
but lovely sleep did not seize Deidameia
as she remembered the name of crafty Odysseus
and of godlike Diomedes, who both
had made her bereft of war-loving Achilles,
winning over his bold heart, that he might come
to the deadly battle-cry; and unbending Fate met him,
which cut short his homecoming, and brought boundless grief
to his father Peleus and to Deidameia herself.
Therefore in her heart boundless dread held her
for her son rushing to the tumult of war,
lest upon grievous sorrow there should come more sorrow.
And Dawn went up the great heaven; and they from their beds
quickly rose; and Deidameia perceived it;
and at once, flung about his broad breast,
she wailed grievously, crying long into the air;
as a cow in the mountains, bellowing endlessly,
seeks her calf in the glens, and about her the long
crests of the steep mountain echo;
so, as she mourned, the lofty hall rang round
on every side from its inmost recesses, and greatly grieving she cried:
“Child, where now has your good mind flown away,
to follow strangers to tearful Ilium,
where many perish in the grievous battle,
though they are skilled in war and cruel fighting?
But you are young, and as yet you do not know the deeds of war
which ward off the evil day from men;
but hearken to me, and stay in your own house,
lest an evil report come from Troy to my ears
that you have perished in the battle; for I do not think
that you will come back here again, turning from the throng;
for not even your father escaped the unseen doom,
but was slain in the war, he who surpassed both you
and the other heroes, and a goddess was his mother,
by the guile and counsels of these men, who urge you too
to go to the grievous strife;
therefore I fear, trembling about my heart,
lest for me too, child, if you perish,
being left bereaved I should suffer cruel woes;
for no worse grief ever comes upon a woman
than when her children perish and her husband too,
and her home is widowed by grievous death;
for at once men shear away her fields
and strip everything and have no regard for justice;
therefore nothing is made more wretched
than a widow in her halls, nor any feebler woman.”
So she cried aloud; but her son addressed her in answer:
“Take courage, my mother, and send away the evil omen;
for no man is slain in war beyond his fated doom;
and if it is fated for me to die for the Achaeans,
let me die, having done some deed worthy of the line of Aeacus.”
So he spoke; and near him came aged Lycomedes,
and addressed him as he longed for battle:
“O strong-hearted child, like your father in might,
I know that you are mighty and strong; yet even so
I fear the bitter war and the grievous wave
of the sea; for sailors are ever near to destruction.
But beware, child, when you come upon a voyage
hereafter, either from Troy or from elsewhere, such as often
we men wander upon the boundless back of the sea,
at the time when the sun joins the misty Goatfish,
casting behind him the Archer, drawer of arrows,
when storms drive on the grievous winter,
or when down the wide stream of Ocean are borne
the stars as Orion goes down toward the darkness;
