And before it the sons of Troy, the children of Laocoon being pitilessly slain, made, gathering together, an empty tomb, over which the tears the father shed, with sightless eyes; and around it the mother, much lamenting, cried over the empty tomb, expecting some other thing still worse, and groaned over the ruin of her husband's folly, and dreaded the blessed ones' wrath; as when about her desolate nest she mourns greatly grieving, in a shadowy glen, a nightingale, whose little children, before they could sing their clear song, the might of a grim serpent has slain beneath its jaws, and set woes upon the mother, and grieving boundlessly she mourns about the empty home, crying aloud; so she lamented over the wretched destruction of her children, mourning about the empty tomb; and with her another woe, very grievous, was, concerning her sightless husband. And she wailed for her dear children and her husband, the ones being dead, the other bereft of the sun; but the Trojans made ready offerings to the immortals, pouring sweet wine, since their hearts hoped to escape the heavy might of the wretched war. But the sacrifices would not burn, and the breath of the fire was quenched, as when from above an ill-sounding rain comes rushing; and bloody smoke gushed up; and all the thigh-pieces fell to the ground trembling; and the altars crashed down; and the libations turned to blood; and tears flowed from the gods, and the temples were wet with gore; and groans were borne from somewhere unforeseen; and the long walls shook and the towers crashed loud, as if grieving; and of themselves the bolts of the gates flew open, crying terribly; and there groaned dolefully night-birds, crying their desolate cry; and all the stars above the god-built city a mist enwrapped, though the gleaming sky was without cloud; and the laurels withered by the temple of Phoebus, that before were flourishing; and wolves and shameless jackals howled within the gates; and very many other things appeared, signs to the children of Dardanus, bringing woe to the city. But no grievous dread came upon the Trojans' hearts as they beheld all the grievous portents through the city; for the Fates cast out the mind of all, that at the feast they might fill up their doom, laid low by the Argives. Alone with steadfast heart and prudent thought was Cassandra, whose word was never unfulfilled, but ever true; yet it was heard, by some fate, as ever empty, that pains might come upon the Trojans. She, when she saw the baleful signs through the city rushing together into one, cried aloud, like a lioness, whom in a thicket a man, eager for the hunt, has wounded or struck, and the heart in her breast rages . . . everywhere over the long mountains, and her fury is unrestrained; so she, with raging heart of prophecy within, came forth from the hall; and her hair streamed over her white shoulders, going down to her back; and her eyes flashed wildly; and beneath her, her neck, like a tree-trunk in the winds, swayed continually all about. And greatly the noble maiden groaned and cried aloud: "Ah, wretches, now we go down into the dark; for around us the city is full of fire and blood and dire doom; everywhere the immortals show tearful portents, and at our feet are the bounds of destruction. Foolish ones, you know not at all your evil fate, but all alike you rejoice in your folly, who have led into the city yourselves the Argives' baleful horse; for it hides within a great woe. But you will not believe me, even if I say much, because the Furies, wroth at the height of the dire marriage about Helen, and the pitiless Fates, dart everywhere through the city; and at a grievous feast you devour your last suppers, befouled with evil gore, already treading the same road as the phantoms of the dead." And one, mocking, spoke a baleful word: "O daughter of Priam, why now does your wanton tongue and ill counsel bid you speak all things empty? Neither does maidenly and pure modesty enfold you, but deadly madness has overrun you; therefore now all mortals ever dishonour you, full of words as you are. Begone, and to the Argives and to yourself foretell your evil prophecy; for soon a more grievous pain awaits you than shameless Laocoon's; for it is not fitting to destroy in folly the dear gifts of the immortals." So spoke one of the Trojans through the city; and so others too reproached the maiden, and said she spoke not aright, because to them woe and the grievous might of Fate stood near at hand; but they, not knowing their destruction, mocking her, kept her from the broad horse; for indeed she longed to scatter all the timbers, or to burn them with consuming fire; and therefore from the pine, as it blazed, taking a brand from the hearth, she rushed on in fury; and in her other hand she bore a two-edged axe; and she made for the baleful horse, that the Trojans might behold the groaning ambush openly; but they swiftly snatched from her hands and cast far off the deadly fire and the iron, and heedless made ready the wretched feast; for the last night was coming upon them. And the Argives within rejoiced, hearing the din of the feasters through Ilium, who heeded not Cassandra, whom they marvelled at, how she was truly knowing the mind and the cunning of the Achaeans. And she, like a leopard in the mountains, vexed, which from the courtyard the dogs and the toiling herdsmen drive swiftly, and she, with savage heart, turning back, retreats, though sore beset; so she rushed from the broad horse, with sore-tried heart, over the coming slaughter of the Trojans; for a very great woe she awaited.

And they throughout the city were feasting; and among them the flutes together with the pipes sounded loud; and on every side song to the dance and a confused din arose of the feasters, such as comes at a banquet and over wine. And one, taking in his hands a brimming cup, drank heedlessly; and his wits grew heavy within; and his eyes whirled round about; and one word upon another he let fall from his mouth, uttering broken speech; and to him in the hall the treasures and the house itself seemed like things in motion; and he thought that all was whirling about the city; and a mist enveloped his eyes; for by strong wine are blurred the sight and the mind of men, when it comes flooding into the wits; and, his head heavy, he spoke a word like this: "Truly in vain the Danaans gathered a great host hither, the wretches, nor accomplished what they devised in their minds, but in just this way they have sped away from our city, like little children or like women." So spoke one of the Trojans, his wits hemmed in by wine, the fool; nor did he perceive destruction at the doors. For when sleep held throughout the city one man and another as they filled themselves with boundless wine and food, then Sinon raised aloft the smoking beacon, showing the Argives the gleam of fire; and about him his heart beat unspeakably within his breast, lest the Trojans see him, the strong Trojans, and all at once be made plain; but they upon their beds slept their last sleep, weighed down with much strong wine; and the others, seeing it, from Tenedos made ready their ships for the voyage. And Sinon himself went near the horse; and softly he called, softly and long, that none among the Trojans might hear, but only the leaders of the Danaans, from whom sleep had wholly flown, in their longing to toil. And they, being within, heard him, and toward Odysseus all bent their ears; and he urged them softly and steadily to come forth; and they obeyed his urging toward battle, and from the horse to the ground they were eager to go down; but in his skill he held back all in their eagerness; and he himself with swift hands of the wooden horse very quietly here and there opened the sides, with his good ashen spear, by Epeius' work. A little he leaned out over the planks, and on every side peered for the Trojans, to see if any were awake; and as when, smitten in heart with grievous hunger, a wolf comes from the mountains, craving food, toward the broad fold of the flock, and shunning men and dogs, who are eager to guard the sheep, goes at ease on his feet over the sheepfold's wall; so Odysseus came down from the horse; and about him the other mighty kings of all the Hellenes followed, descending the ladders in rows, which Epeius had made, paths for the strong chiefs as they went into the horse and came out of the horse. And these then about it came down, one from this side, one from that, like bold wasps, which when a woodcutter has stirred, they all together, roused in heart, pour out from the bough, when they hear the noise; so they, eager, poured out from the horse into the well-built city of the Trojans; and in them the heart beat in their breasts . . . . . . quickly they slew the foe . . . . . . and the others still rowed within the sea; and the ships were borne over the great swell; and Thetis guided their course, sending a fair wind behind; and the heart of the Achaeans was warmed; and swiftly coming to the shores of the Hellespont, there again they beached their ships, and all the gear they took down skilfully, all that ever follows ships. And they, straightway disembarking, hastened to Ilium, silent, as sheep that rush toward the fold from the woodland pasture in the night of autumn; so they, voiceless, went toward the city of the Trojans, all eager to help the chiefs. And they, as wolves, ravening dreadfully in their hunger, fall upon the fold along the long mountains and the woodland while the wretched watchman sleeps, and one upon another slay the sheep within the pen beneath the darkness, and on every side . . . . . . . . . with blood and corpses, and dread destruction arose, though still more of the Danaans were outside; but when all of them had come to the walls of Troy, then, raging, pitilessly they poured into the city of Priam, breathing the might of Ares. And the whole city they found full of war and of corpses; and everywhere the groaning halls burned grievously with fire; and greatly in their hearts they were gladdened. And they too, with evil purpose, rushed upon the Trojans; and in their midst raged Ares and groaning Enyo; and everywhere dark blood flowed over, and the earth was drenched as the Trojans were slain and the allies from foreign lands. Of these some, overcome by chilling death, lay throughout the city in their blood; and others above them fell, breathing out their strength; and others with their hands clutching their entrails wretchedly wandered about the houses; and others, their feet cut off on either side, crawled about the corpses, wailing unspeakably; and of many who longed to fight in the dust the hands were struck off, together with the heads themselves; and as others fled, the ashen spears pierced through their backs clean out at the breast, and of others reached the loins above the privy parts, clean through, where most the point of unwearied Ares brings much pain. And everywhere about the city a grievous howling of dogs arose; and the groaning of slaughtered warriors was piteous; and around all the halls there rang an unspeakable cry; and the groaning wail of women was there, like cranes, when they see an eagle darting on high through the air, and there is in their breasts no bold spirit, but only they twitter long, in fear of the sacred bird; so the women of Troy wailed loud, one here, one there, some starting up from their beds, others to the ground leaping; and they took no more thought of their grievous girdle, but in this very way wandered with only a tunic cast about their limbs; and others had not time to take a veil or a deep robe upon their limbs, but, as the foe came on, trembling, they were fettered in helplessness, their hearts quaking, and only with their swift hands the wretched ones hid their shame; and others grievously tore the hair from their heads, and beat their breasts with their hands, wailing aloud; and others endured the turmoil of the foe face to face, and forgot their fear, eager to help the perishing, their husbands or their children, since great courage necessity gave them. And the wailing roused from sleep the tender-minded infants, whose hearts knew not yet of sorrows; and some breathed out their lives upon others; and they sank down, seeing their doom together with their dreams; and around them the baleful Fates rejoiced wretchedly over the dying. And they, as swine in the house of a wealthy lord who makes ready a boundless banquet for the host, in their thousands were slain; and with the baleful gore was mingled the wine still left in the mixing-bowls; nor was there any who, apart from slaughter, bore the groaning iron, not even one who was very weak; and the Trojans were destroyed. And as beneath jackals or wolves the sheep are slaughtered when, in the rushing of the foul heat at midday, the shepherd not being present, in a shady place in a flock all huddled close together they remain, while he brings milk to his own body, . . . filling their capacious bellies, coming upon all, they drink the black blood, and waiting they destroy the whole flock, and make an evil feast for the wretched herdsman; so the Danaans through the city of Priam one upon another slew, rushing on, in the last fray; nor was there any of the Trojans unwounded, but of all alike the bent limbs were spattered, blackened with much blood. Nor was the strife unwounding for the Argives, but some were struck with cups, others with tables, others, struck on the still-burning hearth with brands, others, pierced with spits, breathed their last, on which there still remained the warm flesh of swine as the breath of consuming Hephaestus seethed about; and others again, by axes and swift hatchets, gasped, laid low in their blood; and from their hands the fingers were cut, when upon the sword they cast their hands, longing to ward off the hateful Fates; and one crushed together the skull and the brain of a comrade with a stone he hurled in the fray; and they, like beasts wounded in the steadings of a herdsman of the field, raged grievously, their wrath awakened beneath the baleful night; and greatly thirsting for Ares about the halls of Priam they raised turmoil, driving one this way, one that; and many also fell by the spears of the Argives; for the Trojans, all who had time in the halls to raise either sword or long spear in their hands, laid low the foe, even though weighed down with wine. And an unspeakable gleam arose through the city, because of the Achaeans many held in their hands the gleam of fire, that in the strife they might see clearly both foe and friends. And then the son of Tydeus, meeting in the fray the spearman Coroebus, son of noble Mygdon, pierced him with his spear through the hollow gullet, where the swift paths of drink and food are. And about the spear black doom overtook him; he fell into the black blood and the throngs of the other dead, the fool, nor had joy of the marriage, for whose sake he had come the day before to the city of Priam . . . . . . and had promised to thrust the Achaeans back from Ilium; but the god did not bring his hope to pass; for the Fates had sent destruction upon him. And with him he slew Eurydamas as he came against him, the son-in-law of good-ashen-speared Antenor, who especially in heart among the Trojans was adorned with wisdom. There too he met Ilioneus, an elder of the people, and drew his terrible sword upon him; and the aged man's limbs were wholly loosed upon his body; and trembling, with both his hands he grasped with one the swift sword, with the other the knees of the man-slaying hero; and he, eager though he was for the fray, either by a delay of his wrath, or because a god urged him, held his sword a little back from the old man, that he might say something, beseeching the swift and mighty man; and he, grievously, cried out in haste; and hateful dread enwrapped him: "I beseech you, whoever you are of the mighty Argives, respect my hands cast about you, and from your grievous wrath cease; for indeed it is great glory for a man to have slain a young and mighty man; but if an old man you slay, there will follow no praise for you for valour; therefore turn your hands away from me toward the warriors, hoping yourself one day to come to like old age." To him as he spoke the son of strong Tydeus answered: "O old man, I hope myself to come to a goodly old age; but while still my strength grows, I will leave none an enemy of my head, but will send them all to Hades, since a noble man is he who wards off the foeman." So speaking, he drove the deadly sword through his throat, the terrible man; and he guided it where, for mortals, toward doom, the dire paths of the life and the blood go swiftest; and dire doom loosed him in death, laid low by the hands of the son of Tydeus. And he, still slaying the Trojans, rushed through the city, raging in his might; and he laid low noble Abas; and he struck beneath his long spear the glorious son of Perimnestus, Eurycoon. And Ajax slew Amphimedon, and Agamemnon the son of Damastor, and Idomeneus Mimas, and Meges took Deiopites. And the son of Achilles, beneath his irresistible spear, destroyed noble Pammon, and struck Polites as he came on, and slew Antiphonus besides; and all these together were sons of Priam; and as he came against him in the fray he laid low noble Agenor; and one upon another he slew of the heroes; and everywhere black destruction appeared of the dying; and he, clothed in his father's valour, raging, slaughtered all he caught. And he himself upon the king of the foe, with evil purpose, came at the altar of the Courtyard-god; and he, when he saw the son of Achilles, knew him at once for what he was, and did not tremble, since himself his heart longed to perish over his own sons; therefore he addressed him, longing to die: "O strong-hearted child of warlike Achilles, slay me, and pity not my wretchedness; for I, having suffered such things and so many, long not to look upon the light of the all-seeing sun, but rather already to perish together with my children, and to forget my grief, baleful, and the ill-sounding turmoil. Would that your father had slain me, before I saw blazing Ilium, when I bore the ransom for slain Hector, whom your father slew for me; but that, I think, the Fates spun out; but you, of my slaughter glut your mighty heart, that I may forget my pains." To him as he spoke the mighty son of Achilles answered: "O old man, you bid me, eager and hasting as I am; for I will not leave you, an enemy, among the living; for nothing is dearer to men than life." So speaking, he cut off the head of the grey old man easily, as one would reap an ear from the dry cornfield in the season of warm summer. And it, with a great moan, rolled far over the ground apart from the other limbs by which a man is moved; and it lay in the black blood and the slaughter of other men . . . in wealth and in lineage and in countless children; for not long for men does glory increase, but somehow reproach rushes upon them unforeseen; and him doom took; and he forgot all his woes. And the swift-horsed Danaans cast Astyanax too from the high tower, and slew his dear life, snatching him from his mother's arms, in anger for Hector, since indeed he had brought woe upon them while he lived; therefore they hated his offspring, and cast his child down from the steep wall, the infant, who knew not yet the strife of war. As when wolves in the mountains, craving food, cast down a calf into a sounding chasm by their ill devising, having cut it off from its mother's milk-rich teats, and she runs wailing for her dear young this way and that, lamenting long, and behind her another evil comes, when lions snatch her up too; so her, grieving boundlessly for her own child, the foemen led, together with the other captive women, the daughter of blameless Eetion, crying terribly. And she, remembering her child and her husband and her father, the dire slaughter, fair-ankled Eetione, longed to die, since for queens it is better to die in war than to wait upon meaner folk; and she cried out a piteous cry, grieving greatly in her heart within: "Come now, cast my body too from the dire wall or from the rocks or into the fire, at once, O Argives; for boundless woes are mine; for the son of Peleus slew my noble father in holy Thebe, and in Troy my glorious husband, who was all things to me, all that my heart desired; and he left me a little child still in the halls, in whom I gloried boundlessly, in whom many hopes the evil and reckless Fate has cheated me of. Therefore now, in my grief, from this much-toiled life take me swiftly away, nor lead me to your homes mingled with the captives, since no longer in my heart is it pleasing to be among men, since a god has destroyed my protectors; and dire grief receives me, left desolate by the Trojans amid hateful pains." So she spoke, longing to sink into the earth; for it is not fitting that those should live whom great glory turned to reproach encompasses; for it is terrible to be an object of others' suspicion. But by force they led her unwilling toward the day of slavery. And others in other houses left their lives, the men; and among them a tearful cry arose; but not in the halls of Antenor, because of him the Argives remembered the lovely hospitality, how he had once entertained in the city and saved godlike Menelaus, come together with Odysseus; to him therefore, showing favour, the best sons of the Achaeans left him alive, and let his possessions be, in reverence for all-seeing Themis and for their friend. And then the noble son of blameless Anchises, having toiled much about the city of god-born Priam with spear and manhood, and having taken the lives of many, when he saw, beneath the grievous hands of the foe, the city ablaze, and the host perishing all together, and boundless wealth; and from the halls the wives dragged out together with their children, no longer did his heart have hope to see his well-walled fatherland, but his mind pondered to escape the great woe. As when on the deep of the sea a man, plying the helm of his ship skilfully, shunning the wind and the wave that rush on from every side in the hateful season of storm, wearies his hand and his heart, and, as the ship goes under and perishes, leaving apart the helm alone, goes onto a little boat, and cares no longer for the freighted ship; so the noble son of wise Anchises, leaving the city ablaze with much fire to the foe, snatched up and bore away his son and his father, the one set upon his broad shoulder with his strong hands, labouring beneath much-enduring old age, the other touching with his soft hand and his feet the ground; and, fearing the deeds of the deadly fray, he led him out of the ill-sounding war; and by necessity he hung clinging, the tender child; and tears poured down his soft cheeks; but he, over the bodies of the dead, leaped much with swift feet, and much in the darkness unwillingly he trod; and Cypris led the way, saving from dire woe her grandson and her child and the man, of her own will; and beneath his hasting feet everywhere the fire gave way; and the breaths of consuming Hephaestus parted asunder; and the spears and the shafts of men fell all vainly to the ground, as many as the Achaeans hurled at him in that tearful war. And then Calchas cried aloud, restraining the host: "Cease against the mighty head of Aeneas to hurl your groaning shafts and deadly spears; for it is fated, by the glorious counsel of the gods, that he, coming to the broad-flowing Tiber from the Xanthus, shall build a holy city, a wonder to men to come, and shall himself rule over far-scattered mortals; and from him a race hereafter shall reign even to the rising and the unwearied setting of the dawn; and for him too it is ordained to be among the immortals, since he is the child of fair-tressed Aphrodite. And for other reasons let us keep our hands from this man, since both the gold and all else that is his possession, which saves a man as he flees to a foreign land, above all these he has preferred his father and his son; and one night has shown us a son to an aged father exceedingly tender, and a parent blameless to his child." So he spoke; and they obeyed, and looked upon him as a god, all of them; and he in haste had gone forth from his city, where his feet bore him busily; and still the Argives plundered the well-built city of Troy. And then Menelaus, with his groaning sword, slew Deiphobus, overtaking him heavy-headed beside the bed of Helen, the wretched man; and she in flight hid herself in the halls; but he, as the blood gushed forth, rejoiced over the slaughter; and he spoke a word like this: "O dog, how I have sent groaning death upon you this day; nor shall bright Dawn find you yet alive among the Trojans, even if you boast to be of Zeus the loud-thundering the son-in-law; but black destruction has received you, flayed grievously beside the halls of my wife; would that even before this I had taken the life of accursed Alexander, meeting him in the fray; then my grief would have been lighter; but he has already gone beneath the chilling gloom, having paid all his due; but you my wife was not, it seems, to profit, since lawless men never escape Themis the undefiled, because she beholds them by night and by day, and on every side over the tribes of men through the air she flies, taking vengeance with Zeus on those who know evil deeds." So speaking, he wrought pitiless destruction on the foe; for the heart raged within his breast, swelling greatly, jealous; and many evil things with bold mind he purposed against the Trojans, which the goddess brought to pass, venerable Justice; for they first did reckless deeds about Helen, and first too violated the oaths, the wretches, when they trampled through the black blood and the sacred things of the immortals, by the transgressions of their mind; therefore afterward the Furies wrought woes for them; therefore some perished before the walls, and others through the city taking their delight at the feast and with their fair-haired wives. And at last Menelaus in the inmost parts of the house found his wife, trembling at the threat of her wedded husband, bold of heart, who, beholding her, purposed to slay her in the jealousy of his mind, had not lovely Aphrodite restrained his might, who struck the sword from his hands and stayed his onrush; for she thrust away his dark jealousy, and beneath roused sweet desire in his heart and his eyes. And upon him came astonishment unlooked for; nor did he longer dare, seeing her conspicuous beauty, to bring the sword upon her neck, but, like a dry log in a wooded mountain, he stood, which neither the swift blasts of the North rushing through the air stir, nor of the South; so he in amazement stood long; and his valour was unstrung as he looked upon his wife; and at once he forgot all, all the wrongs she had done him in his wedded bed; for the goddess Cypris confounded all, who of all the immortals and of mortal men subdues the mind. But even so, raising the swift sword again from the ground, he rushed upon his wife; and his mind in his heart strove with other purpose as he hastened; but with guile he beguiled the Achaeans. And then his brother restrained him, eager though he was, with very many soothing words speaking beside him; for he feared lest all should be made vain for them: "Stay now, Menelaus, your wrath; for it is not fitting to slay your wedded wife, for whose sake many woes we have endured, devising evil for Priam; for Helen is not the cause, as you suppose, but Paris, who forgot the hospitable Zeus and your table; therefore the god has punished him amid woes." So he spoke; and at once he obeyed. And the gods over glorious Troy, covering themselves in dark clouds, lamented, save fair-tressed Tritonis and Hera, who greatly gloried in their hearts, when they saw the famed city of god-born Priam being sacked. Yet not even wise Tritogeneia herself was wholly tearless, since in her temple Ajax, the mighty son of Oileus, had outraged Cassandra, mad in heart and mind; and she upon him a dire woe cast afterward, and avenged the man for the outrage; nor did she look upon the unseemly deed, but shame and wrath were poured about her; and she turned her grim eyes to the high-roofed temple; and the divine image groaned around, and the floor of the temple greatly trembled; but he from the baleful recklessness did not cease, since Cypris had blinded his wits. And everywhere this way and that the halls crashed down from on high; and dry dust mingled with smoke; and a dire crash arose, and the streets trembled; and the house of Aeneas burned, and all the halls of Antimachus burned; and there blazed the boundless height about lovely Pergamus and about the holy temple of Apollo and the sacred shrine of Tritonis and about the altar of the Courtyard-god; and the lovely bridal chambers of the sons of Priam were set ablaze; and all the city was laid in ashes. And of the Trojans some perished beneath the children of the Argives, others beneath the baleful fire and their own halls, where for them was made both evil fate and tomb, and others drove their swords through their own throats, seeing the fire together with the foe at their doors, and others, having slain together with their children their wives, fell, having fulfilled an unbearable deed by necessity. And one, thinking the cry of the foe was far off, took up swiftly a pitcher from the hearth of Hephaestus and was eager to labour at the water; but, forestalling him, one of the Argives struck him with the spear, and took his life, weighed down with strong wine; and he fell within the house; and around him the empty pitcher fell. And upon another, as he fled through the hall, the cross-beam fell, burning, and steep destruction crashed upon him. And many women again, in grievous flight rushing, remembered their dear children beneath the house, whom they had left in their beds; and at once running on their feet they perished together with their children as the houses fell above them. And horses and dogs through the city were panicked, fleeing the might of the hateful fire; and beneath their feet they trampled the slain, and bringing woe to the living they ever crashed against them. And a cry rang about the city. And of some warrior, as he rushed through the flame . . . crying out; and within them pitiless Fate laid them low; and different paths of groaning destruction bore one and another. And the flame rose up to the divine air; and a boundless gleam spread out; and the tribes of the dwellers round about beheld it, even to the high peaks of the Idaean mountains, and of Thracian Samos and of sea-girt Tenedos; and one on the deep of the sea, within his ship, spoke a word: "The strong-hearted Argives have accomplished a boundless deed, having toiled greatly for Helen of the rolling eyes, and all that city, before so wholly blessed, in fire burns; nor did any of the gods defend it in their longing; for boundless Fate looks down on all the deeds of mortals; and many things, inglorious and unconspicuous, she makes glorious, and the lofty she has made less; and often from good comes evil, and from evil good, as much-enduring life is changed about." So spoke one of mortals from afar, beholding the boundless gleam; and groaning misery still enwrapped the Trojans; and the Argives raised turmoil through the city, like winds that, fierce, drive on the boundless sea when it is stirred, when over against the foul-blowing Arcturus the Altar rises to the starry threshold, turned toward the misty south, and about it many ships are destroyed in the sea, sunk beneath, as the winds rise; like these were the sons of the Achaeans as they plundered steep Ilium; and it burned in much fire. As when a mountain, clothed thick all over with woodland, burns swiftly beneath fire roused by the winds, and the long peaks roar round about, and grievously all the wild things are tortured beneath the might of Hephaestus, wheeling about the wood; so the Trojans were slain throughout the city; nor did any of the heavenly ones save them; for everywhere about them the Fates had set their long nets, which no mortal ever escaped. And then to Demophoon and war-steadfast Acamas, through the city, the mother of great Theseus came, Aethra, in her longing; and one of the blessed ones led her, who brought her face to face with them; and she had wandered fleeing from the war and the fire; and they, beholding in the gleam of Hephaestus the form and stature of the woman, said she was the godlike wife of god-born Priam; and at once, in their eagerness, upon her they cast their hands, longing to lead her away to the Danaans; and she, groaning terribly, spoke among them: "Do not, glorious children of the war-loving Argives, dragging me like a foe, lead me to your ships; for I boast not to be of Trojan race, but noble blood is mine, the blood of the Danaans, most glorious, since Pittheus begot me in Troezen; and noble Aegeus wedded me in marriage; and from me came glorious Theseus my son. But me, by great Zeus and by your dear parents, if truly the sons of blameless Theseus have come hither together with the sons of Atreus, show me, to his dear children, in my longing, throughout the host, whom I think to be of like age with you; and my heart will breathe again, if I see them living, both noble chiefs." So she spoke; and they, hearing, remembered their father, all he did for Helen, and how they sacked Aphidnae, the sons of loud-thundering Zeus, before, when from the battle they hid away their nurses, while they were still infants; and they remembered noble Aethra, all she toiled under captive necessity, being at once both a mother-in-law and a handmaid born to godlike Helen; and in their amazement they rejoiced. And noble Demophoon spoke to her in her longing: "For you indeed the gods are fulfilling your heart's desire at once, since you have beheld the sons of the blameless son, even us, who, lifting you in our dear hands, will bear you to the ships, and to the holy soil of Hellas will lead you gladly, where before you were queen." So he spoke; and the mother of his great father embraced him, casting her arms about him, and kissed his broad shoulders and his head and his breast and his bearded chin; and likewise she kissed Acamas, and about them tears sweet flowed down their eyelids as they wept; as when, of a warrior who is among foreign men, the people spread the report of his death, and then his sons, beholding him afterward come home, weep very sweetly; and he likewise with his children himself mourns in the halls upon their shoulders, and about the house a piteous sound of sweet lamenting flies around; so over them as they wept a sweet wailing flamed about. And then they say that the daughter of much-possessing Priam, Laodice, stretched her hands to the air, praying to the unwearied blessed ones, that the earth might swallow her up, before she set her hand to slavish work. And one of the gods heard her, and straightway the earth beneath he rent, boundless; and she, by the promptings of the god, received the divine maiden within a hollow chasm, as Ilium perished, for whose sake they say even deep-robed Electra herself wrapped her body about with mist and clouds, departing from the dance of the other Pleiades, who are indeed her sisters; but they, in the sight of wretched men, rise in their throng to the sky; but she alone is hidden ever unseen, since the holy city of her noble son Dardanus had fallen; nor did Zeus himself, most high, help her from the air, since to the Fates even the might of great Zeus yields; but this, I think, the noble mind of the immortals soon wrought, or they themselves; and the Argives still roused their spirit against the Trojans everywhere through the city; and Strife held the bounds of battle.

And then from Ocean the golden-throned goddess Dawn sprang up to the sky; and Chaos received the night. And the Argives by force laid waste well-fenced Troy and plundered her boundless wealth, like torrent rivers, which are borne from the mountains with a roar when the rain is stirred up, and many tall trees and all that grows in the hills, with the very headlands, they bear into the sea; so the Danaans, having sacked beneath fire the Trojan city, bore all the goods to their swift-bounding ships. And together they drove off the women of Troy from this side and that, some still unwed and inexperienced of marriage, and one new-subdued to love beneath the warriors, others again grey-haired, and others younger than these, whose children they had torn from their breasts, still craving with their lips the last of the milk. Among these Menelaus himself, in their midst, led his own wife from the burning city, having accomplished a great deed; and joy and shame held him. And good-ashen-speared Agamemnon led off noble Cassandra; and Andromache the noble son of Achilles; but Odysseus dragged Hecuba by force; and from her eyes thronging tears, like a spring, poured down; and her limbs trembled, and her heart was distraught with fear, and she had torn her hair from her grey head; and much ash lay upon her, which she had heaped abundantly with her hands from the hearth as Priam perished and the city blazed; and she groaned greatly, when the day of slavery enwrapped her, dragged off against her will; and one led one wailing woman, another another, of the Trojan women, by force to their ships; and they, wailing piteously, cried aloud, one here, one there, lamenting most grievously together with their infant children; as when, together with white-tusked swine, men drive the young from the former steading to another steading in the rising of a storm, and they, grievously mingled together, squeal continually to one another; so the women of Troy, subdued, groaned beneath the Danaans; and queen and handmaid alike bore equal necessity. But Helen no wailing enwrapped; rather shame sat upon her dark eyes, and above her fair cheeks blushed red; and within her the heart beat unspeakably in her breast, lest, as she went to the dark ships, the Achaeans should maltreat her; therefore, trembling, she quivered in her dear heart. And, covering her head above with a veil, she followed in the footstep of her husband as he went, blushing in her cheek for shame, like Cypris, when the heavenly ones, in the embrace of Ares, plainly perceived her dishonouring her own bed in the close-set bonds of skilful Hephaestus, in which she lay, grieving in heart and ashamed before the throng of the blessed ones gathered there, and before Hephaestus himself; for it is terrible, in the eyes of one's husband, to be plainly beheld in shame, for womankind. Like her in form and in undefiled shame went Helen with the captive Trojan women, she too, to the well-oared ships of the Argives; and around her the host marvelled, beholding the splendour and the lovely beauty of the blameless woman; nor did any dare to provoke her, neither secretly with abusive words, nor yet openly, but they looked upon her as a goddess, gladly; for to all in their longing she appeared. And as, to men wandering over the unwearied sea, their own fatherland appears at last to their longing, and they, having escaped both the sea and death, stretch out their hands to their country, rejoicing boundlessly in heart; so all the Danaans around rejoiced; for no longer in them was there memory of grievous toil nor of turmoil; for such a mind Cytherea made in them all, bringing grace to bright-eyed Helen and to Zeus the father. And then, when he saw his dear city laid waste, Xanthus, still breathing the bloody din, mourned together with the Nymphs, since evil had fallen on Troy from somewhere, and laid low the city of Priam; as when the dry cornfield, with hail bearing down, is cut short, and all the ears are stripped away by the grievous blast, and the stalk is poured on the ground, the fruit lost in vain upon the soil, grievously, and great grief comes to the wretched lord; so also to the heart of Xanthus came grief as Ilium was left desolate; and misery held him ever, immortal though he was; and tall Ida groaned around, and Simoeis; and far off all the haunts of Ida mourned, wailing for the city of Priam. And the Argives went to their ships, greatly exulting, hymning the mighty valour of their glorious victory, and now the holy race of the blessed ones, and now their own daring spirit and the imperishable work of Epeius. And song reached the sky through the air, like the cry of jackdaws, boundless, when a fair day comes out of the deadly winter, and the air is calm; so the heart of those by the ships rejoiced greatly within . . . and the immortals throughout the sky took delight, all who were helpers in their hearts of the war-loving Argives; but others were vexed, all who defended the Trojans, beholding the city of Priam ablaze; but they, though longing to help, could not avail beyond Fate; for not even the son of Cronos himself, beyond doom, could easily thrust Fate aside, he who of all the immortals has the most might, and from Zeus all things come. And the Argives, setting on the altars many thigh-pieces of oxen, burned them together with the cleft wood, and hastening about the altars poured sweet wine over the blazing offerings, bringing grace to the gods, since they had accomplished a great deed. And much at the heart-cheering banquet they glorified all who had been received with their arms in the wooden horse; and they marvelled at glorious Sinon, because he had endured the much-grievous outrage of the foe; and all of them honoured him with song and with boundless gifts; and he in his heart rejoiced, with steadfast spirit, at the victory of the Argives, and grieved not at his own outrage; for to a prudent and thoughtful man far better is glory than gold or beauty or any other of the good things that are or shall be for men. And they beside the ships, with fearless hearts, supped, telling each other continually: "We have accomplished the end of the long war; we have won broad glory, having taken with the foe their great city; but, O Zeus, grant us also the return in our longing." So they spoke; but the father did not grant return to all. And among them one, skilled . . . . . . for no longer in them was there dread of the ill-sounding war, but to the works of good order they turned, and to lovely good cheer. And he indeed first, to their longing, sang how the host had gathered to the holy ground of Aulis, and how the great might of unwearied Peleus' son went over the sea and sacked twelve cities, and eleven again over the boundless land, all that he wrought about lord Telephus and mighty Eetion, and how he slew overweening Cycnus, and all that the Achaeans in the wrath of Achilles wrought as they fought, and how he dragged Hector about the walls of his own fatherland, and how he took Penthesileia in the fray, and how he subdued the son of Tithonus, and how strong Ajax slew good-ashen-speared Glaucus, and how the glorious man Eurypylus the son of swift Aeacides slew, and how the shafts of Philoctetes laid low Paris, and all the men who went within the guileful horse, and how, having sacked the city of god-born Priam, they feasted, far apart from evil turmoils. And this man sang one thing, that man another, whatever was in his heart. But when, as they feasted, the middle of night came round, then indeed from supper and from the strong drink all ceased, and took care-banishing sleep; for the strength of yesterday's toil overcame them all; and so, though they had longed to feast all night long, they ceased, since sleep against their will held them fast; and one slept here, another there; but in his own hut the son of Atreus conversed with his fair-haired wife; for not yet had sleep fallen upon their eyes, but Cypris was busy about their hearts, that they might remember their old marriage-bed, and cast their grief away. And first Helen spoke a word like this: "Do not now, O Menelaus, set wrath against me in your heart; for it was not of my own will that I left your home and bed, but the might of Alexander and the sons of Troy snatched me away, coming while you were far off, and, though I was utterly eager to perish wretchedly either by a grievous noose or by a groaning sword, they kept me in the halls, comforting me with words, grieving for you and for my well-loved daughter; by her, then, and by our marriage of much joy and by yourself I beseech you, to forget your hateful anger against me." To her as she spoke wise Menelaus answered: "No longer now remember it, but hold your griefs in your heart; but let the black house of forgetfulness shut all these things within; for it is not fitting to remember evil deeds any longer." So he spoke; and joy seized her, and fear rushed from her heart; for she hoped that her husband would cease from grievous wrath; and she cast her arms about him; and from them both alike sweet tears flowed down their eyelids as they wept. And gladly the two of them, reclining beside one another, remembered in their hearts their own marriage; as when ivy and the cultivated vine cast themselves about one another round the trunks, and never can the force of the wind hurl them apart; so the two of them held to one another, longing for love. But when sleep, free from harm, came upon them too, then the strong heart of godlike Achilles stood over the head of his son, just as he was when alive, when he was a grief to the Trojans, a joy to the Achaeans. And he kissed his neck and his gleaming eyes gladly, and, comforting him, spoke: "Hail, my child, and do not rend your heart with grief because of my death, since with the blessed gods I am now a fellow at the hearth; but restrain your heart, sore-tried for me, and set my strength to the full in your spirit. Ever stand as foremost of the Argives, yielding to none in manhood; but in the assembly to the elder men give heed; and then all will call you wise. Honour the blameless men, all whose mind is steadfast; for to the noble a noble man is dear, and to the harsh, grievous. If you think good thoughts, you will achieve good deeds too; for that man never reached the goals of Virtue who has not a righteous mind; because her trunk is hard to climb, and far up to the clear sky her branches grow; but those whom strength attends and toil, from labour reap the much-rejoicing fruit, having climbed up to the glorious shoot of fair-crowned Virtue. But come, be glorious, and in your prudent wits neither in calamity wholly rend your heart with grief, nor in good fortune greatly rejoice; but let your mind be gentle toward your dear comrades and your sons and your wife, remembering in your heart that near to men are the gates of deadly doom and the houses of the dead; for the race of men is like the flowers of the grass, the flowers of spring; some wither, some grow; therefore be gentle. And to the Argives say, and most of all to Atreus' son Agamemnon, if in heart they remember all I toiled about the city of Priam, and all I plundered before I came to the Trojan soil, let them now, in my longing, lead to my tomb, from the spoil of Priam, fair-robed Polyxena . . . that they may sacrifice her swiftly, since I am wroth at them yet more even than before about Briseis; and the swell of the sea I will stir, and cast storm upon storm, that, wasting away by their own follies, they may remain here a long time, until to me they pour libations in their longing greatly for return; but herself, if they wish, when they have taken her life, the maiden, I do not at all grudge them to bury far off." So speaking, he darted away, like a swift breeze; and at once he went to the Elysian plain, where is made, from the highest heaven, a descent and an ascent for the immortal blessed ones; and he, when sleep left him, remembered his father; and his noble mind was gladdened. But when to the broad sky rose Dawn, scattering the night, and earth and air appeared, then the sons of the Achaeans started up from their beds eager for return, and the ships into the depths of the sea they were dragging, exulting in their hearts, had not the mighty son of Achilles checked them in their haste, and called them to assembly, and spoke his father's command: "Hear me, dear children of the war-steadfast Argives, the charge of my glorious father, which he told me yesterday in my bed as I slept through the darkness; for he said he was among the everlasting immortals; and he bade you and the king, the son of Atreus, that from the war you should lead a most lovely prize, fair-robed Polyxena, to his dank tomb; and he said that, having sacrificed her, you should bury her far off; but if, heedless of him, you should sail the sea, he threatened, raising adverse waves over the deep, to keep the host together with the ships here a long time." So he spoke; and they obeyed, and prayed to him as to a god; for indeed in the deep the wave grew with the storm, broader and more close-set than before, as the wind raged; and the great sea was stirred up by the hands of Poseidon; for to strong Achilles he brought grace; and swiftly all the blasts rushed upon the sea; and the Danaans, praying greatly to Achilles, all together spoke thus to one another: "Truly Achilles was of the race of great Zeus; therefore now too he is a god, even if before he was among us; for deathless time does not blot out the race of the blessed." So speaking, they went back to the tomb of Achilles; and they led her, as a calf to the offerings of an immortal, which the herdsmen have torn from its mother in the thickets, and it, lowing loud, laments, grieving in heart; so then the daughter of Priam wailed bitterly in the hands of the foe; and abundant tears poured from her; as when, beneath a strong press, the fruit of the olive, not yet blackened with the wintry rain, pours much oil, and the gear creaks loud beneath the cords, as the men force it; so also from the daughter of much-enduring Priam, dragged to the tomb of pitiless Achilles, the dire tears, with groans, ran down her eyelids; and her bosom beneath was filled; and her skin was wet, truly like to costly ivory. And then, upon her grievous griefs, a more bitter pain fell into the heart of long-suffering Hecuba; and in her the spirit remembered a wretched and grievous dream, which she had seen sleeping in the night gone by; for indeed she thought that on the tomb of godlike Achilles she stood lamenting, and her hair to the ground was poured from her head, and from both her breasts ran red blood to the earth, and drenched the tomb; fearing for this, and foreseeing great woe, she wailed piteously, and over the lament cried aloud; as when a bitch, lamenting before the house, sends forth a long howling, newly torn from her milk, whose infant young, before they could look upon the light, the masters have cast away, to be prey for the birds, and she, now with whining laments, now again with howling, and a hateful cry rushes through the air; so Hecuba, wailing, cried aloud over her daughter: "Ah me, what first, what last, grieving in heart, shall I wail, encompassed with many evils, my sons or my husband, who have suffered dire and unlooked-for things, or my city or my disgraced daughters, or my own day of necessity and slavery? Because the terrible Fates have entangled me in many evils. My child, for you too, dire and unlooked-for things the Fates have spun, even for yourself; and from your marriage they have cast the Wedding-song, though it was near, and have brought about destruction, unbearable and grievous and unspeakable; for indeed Achilles even in death still warms his heart with our blood; would that, with you, my dear child, on this day the earth had gaped and covered me, before I saw your doom." As she spoke, ceaselessly down her eyelids poured the tears; for she had grief upon grief, grievously. And when they came to the tomb of holy Achilles, then his dear son, drawing his swift sword, with his left hand held back the maiden, and with his right, touching the tomb, spoke a word like this: "Hear, father, your son who prays, and the other Argives, and be no longer grievously wroth with us; for now we will accomplish all that you desire in your heart; but be gracious to us, granting, to us who pray, swiftly a heart-cheering return." So speaking, he drove the deadly sword through the maiden's white throat; and at once the much-loved life left her, as she wailed piteously at the last of her living; and she fell forward to the ground; and beneath her neck all was reddened, like snow, which in the mountains, of a boar or a bear pierced through by a javelin, swiftly grows red above with crimson blood. And the Argives at once gave her to be borne to the city, to the house of godlike Antenor, because he among the Trojans, for his own noble son Eurymachus, had reared her before as his bride. And when he had buried the glorious daughter of Priam near his own house, beside the sacred tomb of Ganymede and over against the temple of the Unwearied One, then the wave ceased, and the storm was lulled, the terrible storm, and calm soothed the swell. And they swiftly went to their ships, greatly exulting, hymning the holy race of the blessed and Achilles. And at once they took their meal, having cut the thighs of oxen for the immortals; and lovely sacrifice was everywhere; and they, in silver and in golden cups, drank, drawing sweet wine; and the heart in them rejoiced, as they longed to come to their own land. But when they had taken their fill of supper and the feast, then the son of Neleus spoke to them in their longing: "Hear, friends, you who have escaped the long din of war, that I may tell a word pleasing to your hearts in your longing; for now is the season of heart-cheering return; but let us go; for indeed the mighty heart of Achilles has ceased from its grievous wrath; and the Earth-shaker has checked the mighty wave; and gentle breezes blow; and no longer does the wave rear up; but come, the ships into the swell of the sea let us draw, and bethink us of return." So he spoke to their longing; and they made ready for the voyage. There a portent, a marvel to men on earth, appeared, because the wife of much-bewept Priam from a mortal became a piteous bitch; and around her the host marvelled, gathering; and all her limbs to stone a god turned, a great wonder even for men to come; and her, by the promptings of Calchas, the Achaeans set on a swift ship across the Hellespont. And swiftly, drawing their ships into the sea, they cast in all the goods, all that, coming to Ilium, they had plundered before, having subdued the dwellers round about, and all that they brought from Ilium itself, in which most they rejoiced, since they were very many; and with them many captive women followed, sorely grieving in heart; and they themselves came within the ships. But to them Calchas did not follow as they hastened into the sea, but the other Argives too he kept back; for about the Capherean rocks he feared a dire destruction rushing upon the Danaans. But they obeyed him not at all; for an evil fate beguiled the minds of men; and alone, well knowing the prophecies, Amphilochus, the swift son of blameless Amphiaraus, remained together with wise Calchas; for to them it was fated, both of them, far from their own land, to the cities of the Pamphylians and Cilicians to come. But these things the gods set for afterward; and the Achaeans loosed their ships' cables from the land, and their anchors swiftly raised; and the Hellespont rang as they hastened; and the ships were washed about by the sea; and around them, about the prows, lay many arms of the slain; and above, tokens of victory, countless, were hung aloft; and they crowned the ships both with garlands and with spears and with shields, with which they fought against the foe; and from the prows the lords poured into the dark sea much wine to the gods, praying to the blessed ones to grant a return free from grief; and their prayers were mingled with the winds, and far from the ships in vain were borne off together with the clouds and the air. And the captive women gazed back toward Ilium, grieving in heart, and much, lamenting, they wailed, hiding from the Argives the great grief in their hearts; and some held their hands about their knees; and others their foreheads propped upon their hands, the wretched ones; and others their children held in their arms; and these did not yet groan for the day of slavery nor for their fatherland's woes, but at the breast held their hearts; for far from sorrows is an infant's heart. And the hair of all was loosed, and their grievous breasts were torn about with their nails; and on their cheeks the tears lay dry, and others above flowed down thick from their eyelids; and they beheld their wretched fatherland still wholly ablaze, and the much smoke rising; and about glorious Cassandra, gazing, they all looked, remembering her grievous prophecy; and she laughed at them as they wailed, though grieving herself at the hateful woes of her fatherland. And of the Trojans, all who escaped from the pitiless war, gathering through the city, laboured about the corpses, eager to bury them; and to the grievous work Antenor led them; and on a single pyre they laid many. And the Argives, exulting ceaselessly in their hearts, now with their oars clove the dark water, now with eager haste made ready the sails on their ships; and behind them swiftly was left all Dardania and the tomb of Achilles; and they in their hearts, though rejoicing, remembering the slain, with one mind grievously grieved, and toward a foreign land they cast their eyes. And it appeared to them far from the ships, receding; and they swiftly were borne past the surf of sea-girt Tenedos; and they passed Chryse and the holy seat of Sminthian Phoebus and divine Cilla; and windy Lesbos appeared; and they rounded the cape swiftly of Lectum, where is the last headland of Ida. And the swelling sails roared round; and about the prows the dark swell crashed; and the long waves were darkened; and the sea-paths whitened over the deep. And now the Argives would have come to the holy soil of Hellas, all of them, over the deep of the sea unharmed, had not the daughter of loud-thundering Zeus, Athena, been wroth with them; and when they came near windy Euboea, then, devising a heavy and pitiless doom for the king of the Locrians, and chafing unbearably, she stood beside Zeus, lord of the gods, and spoke a word apart from the immortals; and her heart could not contain its wrath: "Father Zeus, no longer are the deeds men devise endurable to the gods, men who heed in their minds neither yourself nor the other blessed ones, since now vengeance no longer follows wretched men, but often the noble man is borne down more by woes, and has unceasing misery; therefore no one any longer reveres justice, nor is there shame among men; I for my part will neither in Olympus be, nor be called yours any longer, unless of the Achaeans I take vengeance for their recklessness, since indeed within my temple the son of Oileus greatly transgressed against me, nor did he pity Cassandra, stretching her heedless hands toward me many times, nor did he fear my might, nor in his heart did he reverence the immortal, but wrought an unbearable deed. Therefore now, in your immortal heart, do not grudge me to do as my spirit desires, that others too, the warriors, may tremble at the gods' clear threat." To her as she spoke the father answered with gentle words: "My child, I in no way oppose you for the sake of the Achaeans, but all the gear, which before, bringing grace to me, with their unwearied hands the Cyclopes fashioned, I will give you in your longing; but you, with your strong heart, yourself stir a grievous storm upon the Argives." So speaking, the swift lightning and the deadly thunderbolt and the groaning thunder, near the fearless maiden he set; and her heart was greatly gladdened within. And at once she put on the rushing aegis, all-gleaming, unbreakable and strong and a wonder to the immortals; for upon it was wrought the head of grim Medusa, terrible; and strong serpents, breathing the rush of unwearied fire, fierce, were above it; and the whole aegis rang about the breast of the queen, as when the boundless sky roars with the lightnings. And she took her father's arms, which no god lifts save great Zeus; and she shook tall Olympus; and she poured together the clouds and all the air above; and night was poured about the earth, and the sea grew dark; and Zeus looked on and greatly rejoiced; and the broad sky moved about the feet of the goddess; and the air rang round, as when unwearied Zeus rushes eagerly to the fray. And straightway, to be borne over the misty sea, she sent from heaven to Aeolus immortal Iris, that he might send all the winds together, bearing down, to come near the rugged heights of Caphereus, ceaselessly driven, and to swell up the sea, maddened with grievous blasts. And she, hearing, swiftly darted, wrapped about with clouds; you would have said there was fire together with the air and the black water. And she came to Aeolia, where, of the winds that blow fierce, the caves are, fitted about with hard rocks, hollow and echoing; and close by are the halls of Aeolus, son of Hippotas. And she found him within with his wife and twelve children; and she told him all that Athena was devising against the return of the Danaans. And he did not disobey, but, going outside the halls, with his unwearied hands he struck a great mountain with his trident, where the winds, loud-sounding and ill-sounding, were housed in a hollow cavern; and ever a cry rang round, bellowing grievously; and by force he broke the height. And they at once poured out; and he bade them all, gathering a dark tempest together, to blow, that the grievous swell of the rising sea might cover the heights of Caphereus. And they swiftly arose before they heard from their king all his word; and as they rushed, the sea groaned unbearably; and like to steep mountains the waves were borne, one here, one there. And the heart of the Achaeans was broken in their breasts, since the wave now bore the ship high through the air, and now again bore them, as if rolling down a cliff, into the misty depths; and a force unbearable ever spurted up the sand as the surge parted. And they, smitten with helplessness, neither upon the oar could lay a hand in their dismay, nor the sails, strong though they longed, could haul up about the yards, as they broke from the winds, nor steer back again to the voyage; for grievous storms drove on around them; nor had the helmsmen any longer strength of the ships with their skilled hands swiftly to ply the steering-oars; for all things this way and that the evil blasts confounded. Nor was there any hope of life, because dark night together with the great storm and the dire wrath of the immortals arose; for Poseidon stirred up the pitiless sea, bringing grace to his brother's glorious daughter, who herself too, from above, raging pitilessly, rushed amid the lightnings; and Zeus thundered from heaven, glorifying his child in his heart; and all around the islands and the mainlands were flooded by the sea, not far from Euboea, where most the deity wrought, upon pitiless griefs, fresh griefs, for the Argives. And groaning and wailing throughout the ships arose of the perishing; and the timbers of the ships crashed as they broke; for they, crowded close upon one another, ever shattered together; and toil unending arose. And some, eager with their oars to thrust off the ships that rushed upon them, with the very timbers, wretched, fell into the great deep, and beneath pitiless doom died, because upon them from this side and that bore down the long timbers of the ships; and the bodies of all were crushed together grievously; and others, fallen in the ships, lay like to the dead; and others, by necessity, swam, clinging to the well-polished oars; and others again floated upon the planks; and the brine roared from the depth, so that the sea and the sky and the land too appeared all joined together to one another. And she of Olympus, the loud-thundering Unwearied One, in no way shamed her father's might; and around her the air rang. And she, bringing wrath and woe to Ajax, cast a thunderbolt upon his ship; and at once, this way and that, she scattered it in little pieces; and earth and air rang round; and all of encircling Amphitrite was swept over. And they fell out of the ship in a throng; and around them the long waves were borne; and in the lightnings of the queen a gleam flashed, darting through the darkness; and they, gulping the undrinkable brine of the much-sounding sea, breathing out their lives, were borne over the deep. And to the captive women, even as they perished, came joy; and some of them sank into the sea, casting their arms about their children, the wretched ones; and others grievously cast their hands about the heads of the foe, with whom, baleful, they hastened to perish, taking vengeance on the Danaans, worthy of their own outrage; and she, looking down from above, rejoiced in her heart, noble Tritogeneia. And Ajax now swam about a timber of the ship, now again with his hands traversed the briny depths, like to the unwearied Titan in his overweening might; and the briny swell was cloven about the strong hands of the high-hearted man; and the gods, beholding him, marvelled at his manhood and strength; and about him the wave now bore him huge, as upon the peak of a high mountain through the air, now again from on high, as in ravines, hid him; but he his hands wearied not, much-enduring; and many on this side and that, quenched, the thunderbolts crackled into the sea; for not yet did the daughter of loud-thundering Zeus devise to subdue his spirit with doom, much though she was wroth, before he had endured many evils and toiled utterly in griefs; therefore in the deep misery long laid him low, tormented on every side; for round about boundless evils the Fates set about the man; but necessity breathed strength into him; and he said that, even if all the Olympians came together into one, in wrath, and raised the whole sea, he would escape; but in no way did he escape the gods' threat; for the overweening Earth-shaker was wroth with him, when he saw him clinging with his hand to the rock of Gyrae, and he was greatly enraged at him; and he shook the sea together with the boundless land; and everywhere round the cliffs of Caphereus were thrown into turmoil; and the grievous surf, beaten, crashed with the fierce swell of the wrathful lord; and he broke off into the sea a broad rock, which that man was grasping with his hands. And as he writhed about the crags for a very long while, his hands were stripped, and blood ran beneath his nails; and the murmuring wave ever, as it was stirred about him, whitened with foam his head and shaggy chin; and now he would have escaped his evil doom, had not against him . . . breaking the earth beneath, he hurled up a peak; as before, against great Enceladus, wise Pallas, lifting up the Sicilian island, cast it down, which still ever burns beneath the unwearied Giant breathing smoking fire within the earth; so the king of the Locrians the height of the mountain covered, the wretched man, falling down from above, and weighed down the strong man; and about him black destruction of death came upon him, subdued together by land and by the barren sea. And so also the other Achaeans were borne over the great gulf, some on their ships in dismay, others fallen outside the ships; and deadly misery held them all; for some of the ships were borne sidelong in the sea, others, turned over, with keel uppermost; and of some the masts were broken off from the beams as the wind drove on; and of others the swift storms scattered all the timbers; and others into the great deep sank beneath, as the boundless rain bore down, nor did they withstand the fierce water of the sea together with the rain of Zeus, mingled; for like a river the air flowed unceasing; and below the divine sea raged. And one said: "Surely such a storm came upon men once, when the unspeakable rain of Deucalion came, and the earth became sea, and the deep poured over all." So spoke one of the Danaans, dismayed in heart at the storm, grievous; and many perished; and about the dead the great swell of the sea was filled, and all the shores were thronged; for the wave spat out many onto the dry land; and about the ships' timbers all of heavy-roaring Amphitrite it covered utterly; and the wave appeared in the midst. And one drew this evil doom, another that; some over the broad sea, as the brine was stirred, unbearable, and others on the rocks, having shattered their ships, perished wretchedly by the contriving of Nauplius; for he, greatly wroth for his son, as the storm arose and the Argives perished, though grieving, greatly rejoiced, because to him the god granted vengeance swiftly, and he saw the hated throng tormented in the deep, and to his own father much he prayed that all might perish together with the ships, sunk beneath. And Poseidon heard him well, and brought them all near the dark swell; and he, like a mountain-mule, with his hand a pine, blazing, raised aloft; and by guile he brought the Achaeans near, hoping to reach the well-harboured seat of havens; for terribly about the hard rocks they were subdued, with their very ships; and upon their evil a more bitter pain they endured, dashed against the grievous rocks in the swift night; and few escaped doom, whom there saved either a god or some helping deity; but Athena now in her heart greatly rejoiced, now again grieved for wise Odysseus, because he was to suffer many pains by the threat of Poseidon, who then, in his unwearied heart utterly grudging the walls and towers of the mighty Argives, which they had toiled to make a defence against the hateful war-cry of the Trojans, swiftly flooded the whole sea over them, all that comes down from the Euxine to the Hellespont, and cast it on the shores of Troy; and from above rained Zeus, bringing grace to the glorious Earth-shaker; nor indeed was the Far-worker free from toil, but from the Idaean mountains all the streams he gathered into one place, and flooded the work of the Achaeans; and the sea was swept over, and still the roaring torrents went, grievously swollen with the rain of Zeus, which the dark swell of much-groaning Amphitrite kept back from coming over the sea, before they had laid in ashes all the walls of the Danaans grievously; and Poseidon himself broke the earth beneath, and there gushed up boundless water and mud and sand; and with his strong might he shook Sigeum; and the shores roared loud, and the foundations of Dardania, and, made unseen and sunk beneath, the boundless rampart was hidden, and it sank within the earth as it parted wide; and the sand alone still appeared as the sea drew back, and from the loud-roaring shores it was stretched out, far from the beach. But these things, I think, the evil purpose of the immortals accomplished; and they in their ships, the Argives, sailed, all whom the storm had scattered; and one came one way, another another, where the god led each, all who over the sea escaped the baleful blasts.
